PREFACE Maize (Zea mays L) is one of the most versatile and multi utility crops, having wider adaptability in diverse ecologies. Globally, it is known as queen of cereals because of its highest genetic potential. It is the major source of food, feed, fodder and industrial raw material and provides enormous opportunity for crop diversification, value addition and employment generation. Maize is also grown for many other special purposes viz. quality protein maize, sweet corn, baby corn, pop corn, waxy corn, high oil and high amylase corn. It is also a solution for various stresses like weed and lowering water table and abiotic stresses like drought, terminal heat, cold, etc. besides providing opportunity for farm mechanization and conservation agriculture and consequently increasing the resource-use efficiency and farm profitability. Presently, maize production is 21.8 million tons and projected demand of maize to be 45 million tonnes by 2030. This demand of maize will be met either by technological intervention or by bringing more area under maize cultivation. The technological interventions for meeting this demand will be adoption of high yielding single cross hybrids seeds, biotechnological intervention and improved package of practices in different agro-ecological regions of the country. It is now well established the adoption of appropriate management practices may prove favourable for sustaining crop productivity and reducing ecological hazards. now well established the adoption of appropriate management practices may prove favourable for sustaining crop productivity and reducing ecological hazards. There is a scope of manipulating production technologies in respect of crop diversification, resource conservation, insect-pest control for improving crop yields on sustainable basis. To make farming sustainable and economically viable, there is a need for rethinking, planning and management in order to face the emerging challenges. Research on maize production systems has therefore provided exciting opportunities for improving input use efficiency, productivity and sustainability. Innovative practices are being attempted to improve productivity, resource-use efficiency and livelihood security. Model training was organized at Directorate of Maize Research, New Delhi to educate the extension workers, agricultural officers, technical personnel etc. of different states in India with regards to all aspects of maize cultivation. This training was attended by 34 personnel from 14 states and eminent experts were invited to deliver lectures. A feedback was also obtained from the participant and they demanded to provide the covered topics which were important from farmer’s point of view in the form a book and with publication of this book the gap has been filled. In this book we included 26 important chapters on various aspect of maize including production technology, input management, conservation agriculture, crop diversification and intensification, crop improvement, plant protection, fodder preservation, specialty corn, diversified uses maize and extension approaches for technology dissemination. We are sure that extension workers will further disperse this information to the benefit of the farmers. In addition to this, it will also helpful as updated knowledge bank to researchers, students and policy makers in maize research, teaching and extension. Editors

Maize and its diversified uses Corn silk Tea brewed from corn silk is used as a remedy for urinary tract infections, as it has diuretic properties. The tea has been marketed to help everything from bedwetting to diabetes to cancer, but the medical community says there is insufficient evidence for such claims. Corn silk is not harmful to most people, but there are some warnings for those with some health conditions or who are taking certain medications. Corn cobs Corn cobs might seem like the throw away part of corn, but have their uses and more uses are discovered or developed all the time. Grinded are used for livestock feed. Traditional farm uses include animal bedding, toilet paper substitute, landfill, fuel and to make corn cob jelly. Modern industrial products made from corncobs include absorbents for oil and hazardous waste, insecticides, fertilizer, and grit for tumbling and blasting. Cobs, as well as corn stalks, are starting to be used to produce ethanol. In addition, you can still make a pipe out of a corn cob. Corn oil Oil is produced by squeezing the germ of the corn. It is used as a food ingredient and for frying food in (most appropriately for popping popcorn). Margarine is often made from corn oil, although other oils are used as well. Corn oil is also used in many cosmetics, soaps, medicines, and other products. 3

AGR 211 (2+1): Crop Production Technology-I Lecture-1 Introduction and importance of cereal crops 1

Cereal? Ø Cereals are the grasses belongs to Gramineae/ Poaceae family grown for their edible grains which composed of endosperm, germ and bran are called as cereals. Ø The word cereals has been derived from ‘Ceres’, name of a Roman Goddess, means ‘Giver of Grains’. 2

Importance of cereals Ø Cereals such as rice, wheat and maize are the important staple food crops in many areas of the world. Ø Approximately 50% of the world's calories are provided by rice, wheat and maize, but in many parts of Africa and Asia, people rely mainly on sorghum or millet. Ø Maize, sorghum and barley are important sources of livestock feed, and barley and rice are used in the brewing industry. Ø Grains of oats in particular, have been shown to contain chemical compounds that help to reduce the chance of certain types of cancer and coronary heart disease. 3

Ø Cereals are the major source of carbohydrates, protein and minerals. Ø Cereals can be found living in a wide range of altitudes (edge of the sea to 1000's of feet above sea level), temperatures (equatorial belt to arctic and Antarctic regions), moisture conditions, soil types and salinity concentrations. Ø Cereals are also used to produce animal feed, oils, starch, flour, sugar, syrup, processed foods, malt, alcoholic beverages, gluten and renewable energy. 4

Nutritive value of cereals Ø Useful amount of protein (gluten) – growth. Ø Small amount of unsaturated fat. Ø Lot of carbohydrates, cellulose, starch, energy. Ø Vitamin B group for nerves and energy. Ø Phosphorous and calcium for bones and iron for the blood. Ø Very little water so they are easy to store. 6

Reasons for low yield of traditional varieties Ø Poor genetic yield potential of the varieties of different crops. Ø Weak and tall straw, susceptible to lodging under heavy fertilizer application. Ø Inefficient leaf arrangement responsible for poor photosynthetic activity and less utilization of Solar energy. Ø Many associated attributes like unsynchronized, susceptibility towards the attack of pests and diseases. 7
In recent years due to all round efforts of agricultural scientists it has been possible to cultivate HYVs of cereal crops which are often been termed as “NEW PLANT TYPES (NPT’s)”. 8

CHARACTERS OF NPT’s : 1. Morphologically dwarf in growth habit with hard and stiff straw. 2. Erect and dark green leaves remaining active for longer duration. 3. Agronomically highly responsive to heavy fertilizer application 4. Physiologically be well equipped for more dry matter production and high yields. 5. Adaptable under different agro climatic conditions and are shorter growing duration. 9

Important features of such NPT’s of cereals in grain crops 1. DWARFNESS: Ø N PT ’s are dw arf in nature d u e t o N O R I N i n w h e a t a n d DEE-GEE-WOO-GEN in rice dwarf genes. Ø NPT’s are short, stiff, not more than knee height but could take more fertilizers without lodging. 10

2. EFFICIANT LEAF ARRANGEMENT: Ø NPTs are narrow, thick, erect and dark green color with optimum LAI composed of properly arranged leaves, which remain active for longer period after flowering due to high sunlight interception they play important role in supporting grain formation resulting into more number of fertile grains per ear head. 11

3. SYNCHRONOUS TILLERING: The growth and development of NPTs are more or less rhythmic i.e., Ø high germination % Ø formation of all tillers at a time (during a specific period) and timely maturity of all the tillers. v So, they have highest synchronized coefficient as regards to the development and maturity of grains of different ears of a plant. 12

4. LOW FLORET STERILITY: Ø Traditional tall varieties under heavy fertilizer application produce more sterile florets. Ø NPT’s have a very low floret sterility % due to synchronized tillering into uniform ear head formation supported by longer physiological activity of leaves at maturity. Ø Low floret sterility an in NPT’s has also been attributed due to increased activities of roots at grain formation stage. 13

5. SHORTER GROWTH DURATION: Ø NPT’s have shorter duration than traditional varieties. Ø At High N application longer growth duration and at low N application, short duration variety is preferred for obtaining higher dry matter production as well as more grain production efficiency i.e., grain yield/unit area/unit time. Ø These short duration varieties can fit very well in under high cropping intensity programmes like multiple and relay cropping. 14

6. ADAPTABILITY TO DIFFERENT CROP SEASONS Ø All most all NPT’s are photo insensitive and completely resistant to fluctuations in day length. Ø They can be grown under all crop seasons provided inputs like fertilizers and irrigations are adequately made available, so higher yields can be obtained. Ø However, some of the NPTs are thermo-sensitive and are affected by variation in temperature during season. Hebbal Avare-4 15

7. ABSENCE OF SEED DORMANCY: Ø NPTs have no dormancy i.e. they do not require any rest period, called dormancy period. Ø Freshly harvested seed can be used for sowing. Ø This character is useful in seed multiplication programmes of HYVs, within a short span of time. Ø This along with photo insensitivity makes them quite suitable for Ø adaptation under high intensity cropping programmes. 16

8. EFFECTIVE TRANSLOCATION OF FOOD MATERIAL FROM PLANTS TO GRAIN Ø NPTs have higher potentiality to absorb and assimilate nutrient from soil throughout the growth duration which in combination with higher photosynthetic activities enable them for higher dry matter production. Ø The built in efficient plant mechanism in NPT’s coupled with fewer organs respiring at flowering stage permit more efficient use of respiration for growth and grain production. Ø After flowering, this enables effective translocation of accumulated food materials of straw for grain formation. 17

9. RESPONSIVE TO HEAVY FERTILISER APPLICATIONS: Ø NPT’s possess the trait of high responsiveness towards fertilizer application. Ø Their optimum N requirement is 2 ½ -3 times more than the requirement is so called improved local varieties similarly, the P & K requirement of NPT’s are also 1 ½ -2 times more in comparison to local types. Ø NPT’s require about 100-120 kg N, 50-70 kg P O and 40-60 kg K O/ha 2 5 2 under optimum conditions of soil moisture status. 18

10. LODGING RESISTANCE: Ø NPT’s are generally dwarf in growth habit with strong and stiff stem which provides them considerable resistance against plant lodging. Ø Because of incorporation of dwarfing genes in NPT’s, they possess the trait of high responsiveness towards heavy fertilizer application without lodging. 19

11. YIELDING POTENTIALITY: Ø The NPT’s are known for their HY potential. Ø NPT’s are capable of yielding 2-3 times more grain yield in comparison to local tall improved types. Ø This is probably due to their altered morphology which results into efficient utilization of water, nutrients and radiation and increased metabolic activities with high dry matter production. Ø Their grain to straw ratio is approximately about 1:1. 20

12. DISEASE SUSCEPTIBILITY: Ø The only drawback associated with NPT’s is the disease susceptibility with luxuriant vegetative growth; the varieties offer scope for insect pests and diseases. However, attempts are being made to develop disease resistant NPT’s. Eg : Rice - BPH resistant varieties: MTU-2067, MTU-2077 and MTU-4870. Wheat ----- Rust resistant varieties ----- Sonalika. 21

Rice ecosystems Rice ecosystem is broadly classified in to 4 types 1. Irrigated ecosystems 2. Rainfed lowlands 3. Rainfed uplands 4. Deep water rice/flood prone 15

1. Irrigated ecosystems Ø It accounts for 49.50% of the total area under rice crop in the country. Ø This system is followed in regions of assured water supply Ø In this system fields are bunded and soils are puddled. Ø Seedlings are transplanted in soft mud under impounded water Ø Water stagnation is continuous throughout the crop growth Ø Raising nursery is indispensible Ø Average yield is 4-5t/ha Major problem: Yield instability and environment Degradation due to inefficient irrigation and nutrient use 16

2. Rainfed low lands Ø Practiced in areas with rainfall of >1000 mm and scope for irrigation is limited. Ø Fields are bunded to store rain water and puddled. Ø Seedlings are transplanted in standing water (30-90 cm depth). Ø Field are not artificially irrigated. Ø It is followed in heavy rainfall hilly regions. This ecosystem is further classified in to 3 types Shallow water : < 50 cm Semi deep water : 50-100 cm Deep water : > 100 cm 17

3. Rainfed upland ecosystem Ø It accounts for 13.5% of the total area under rice crop in the country Ø The areas lies in eastern zone comprising of Assam, West Bengal, north eastern hilly region etc. Ø Upland rice is mostly grown as direct seeded. Ø Fields are unbunded and rain water is not stored Ø It is followed in assured rainfall tracts without irrigation Constraints: Productivity is very low <1.00 t/ha due to uncertainty of available water, light textured and unfertile soil, poor nutrition balance, weed problem 18

4. Deep water rice Ø It accounts for 11.4% of the total area under rice crop in the country. Ø It is followed in an area of very heavy rainfall regions (>2000 mm) Ø Rice seeds are broad casted before the occurrence of rainfall with suitable tolerant varieties Ø Very heavy rainfall leads to flooding of land to a height of 1- 5m Ø This stagnated water is used for fish farming Ø Yield is <1.5 t/ha and variable 19

Climatic condition Ø Rice is a short day plant Ø Among various climatic factors, solar radiation, temperature, rainfall and relative humidity plays a major role in rice production. Rice crop is being cultivated under widely varying climatic conditions as detailed below: Ø Latitude : 45o N – 40o S Ø Altitude : Mean Sea Level to 3000 m MSL Ø RH : 35 – 100% Ø Rainfall : 500mm to 5000mm Ø Temperature : 20o -35o C, night temp: 15-200 is favourable Ø Day length : 9 hrs. optimum Ø Light : 400 cal/cm2/day is the minimum requirement. 21

Botanical description of rice Roots: ØRice form a fibrous root system consisting of seminal, nodal and lateral roots. Seminal Roots: Shortly after germination embryonic roots appear from coleorhiza which may die later. Nodal roots: also called as secondary roots which arises from first node of coleoptile Lateral roots: these roots are called as adventitious fibrous roots which develops from coleoptile. 22

Stem: Ø The stem of rice is called as Culm/ haulm. Ø The culm is made up of a series of nodes and internodes Ø The stem of rice is generally erect, cylindrical and hollow at the internodes and solid at the nodes. 23

Leaf: Ø The node or nodal region of the culm will bear a leaf. Ø Leaves are borne alternately on the culm in opposite directions. One leaf is produced at each node. Ø The topmost leaf below the panicle is the flag leaf. Ø The flag leaf contributes largely to the filling of grains because it supplies photosynthetic products, mainly to the panicle. Ø Most leaves possess small, paired ear-like appendages on either side of the base of the blade - called auricles. Ø ligule a papery membrane at the inside juncture between the leaf sheath and the blade 24

Inflorescence: Ø Inflorescence of the rice is called as panicle. Ø Panicle consists of more number of spikelet Ø Spikelet consists of two hard glumes called Lemma and Palea Ø Lemma and palea leter harden to become Hull or Husk 25
Ø The spikelet/ floret consists of 6 long stamens and a short pistil and at the base two transparent structure called Lodicules. 26

Pollination: Ø Rice is a self pollinated crop Ø On full growth of spikelt, lodicules attains turgidity and push the lemma and palea to open the stamens out of glumes. Ø Later, anthers shed the pollen directly on stigma which facilitates self pollination. ØAfter pollination, grain enters milking stage and then become hard to form a grain. ØThe grain of rice is called as Caryopsis. 27

Growth stages of rice Growth stages of rice is divided in to three types viz., 1. Vegetative stage: it is divided in to 3 sub stages a. Seedling (sowing to transplanting) b. Active vegetative stage (Transplanting to maximum tillering stage) c. Vegetative lag phase (Maximum tillering to panicle initiation) 2. Reproduction stage (PI to flowering) 3. Ripening stage (Flowering to harvest)

a. Seedling stage: Ø Germination to transplanting. Seed germinating to time when young plants becomes independent of food reserve of the seed i.e. nursery stage. Ø The seedlings are transplanted to the main field from nursery at 20-25 days.

b. Active Vegetative Stage (Transplanting to Max. tillering stage): This includes sub stages viz., a) Recovery stage b) Rooting stage c) Maximum tillering stage Ø The transplanted seedlings requires about 9 days to recover from the shock of uprooting during transplanting after which new roots appear. It is also known as recovering and rooting stage.

c) Maximum tillering stage: Ø After recover from transplanting shock, plants start establishing roots, once roots established tillers develop rapidly and increases to a maximum number. Ø Tiller height and straw weight also increases during this stage. Ø Plants attain maximum tillering stage at 25-30 days after transplanting.

C. Vegetative lag phase (Maximum tillering to panicle initiation): It includes sub stages (i) Effective tillering stage Ø During this stage weak tillers begin to die; each strong tiller bears a panicle primordium. Ø The number of these potential productive (ear bearing) tillers come to be fixed at this stage which is known as “Effective tillering stage”.

(ii) Non effective tillering stage Ø Tillers that develop subsequently do not bear panicles and die ultimately. This is the “non effective tillering stage”. Ø Plants reaches panicle initiation stage after 30 days after maximum tillering.

2. Reproductive stage (PI to Flowering): 30 DAS from PI Ø Panicle initiation stage- beginning of reproductive stage. Ø Internodes elongation and booting stage- After panicle initiation internal auxin concentration accelerates and elongates of internodes.

Ø Heading stage: 15 days after booting- emergence of panicle and flowering. Ø Flowering: 20-25 days after booting- continues until the spikelets in the panicle bloom. Followed by pollination and fertilization.

3. Ripening State (Flowering to harvest): 30 Days from flowering This includes the sub stages of grain viz., Ø Milking stage: 7-12 days after anthesis, the water content of the grain turn milky in consistency Ø Dough stage: the grains turn into soft dough stage and later turns into hard dough stage 2-3 weeks after maturity stage. Ø Maturity stage: Grains turn hard and free from greenish Milking Dough Maturity

Ø During vegetative growth period, a relatively small amount of water is needed. Ø Therefore, shortage at this period does not greatly affect the yield, except at the recovering and rooting stages. Ø Stages after panicle primordial development, especially booting, heading and flowering stages need sufficient water.

Systems of cultivation/ Method of cultivation Ø Transplanted irrigated rice Ø Direct seeded rice (DSR) Ø System of rice intensification (SRI) Ø Aerobic rice cultivation

Transplanted irrigated rice Important cultivation practices of transplanted rice includes Ø Nursery Management Ø Puddling Ø Transplanting of seedlings Ø Nutrient management Ø Weed management Ø Water management

Puddling Ø Mechanical manipulation of the soil at high moisture regime (standing water) which reduces deep percolation loss of water is termed as PUDDLING. Ø Puddling of the soil results in the reduction of macro pore space (break down of soil aggregates) and transforming the upper soil layer into a fine soft mud or puddle. Ø It can be done by ploughs, tiller or tractor drawn implements depending upon their availability and soil conditions.

Objectives of Puddling 1. To obtain a soft soil layer for the seedlings to establish themselves faster. 2. Suppression of weeds. 3. To mix organic matter with the soil. 4. To create an impervious sub soil layer for reducing deep percolation & leaching losses of water and nutrients. 5. To facilitate easy transplantation.

Sequential chemical changes that occur during submergence and puddling in rice Ø Chemical reduction of soil, characterization of the oxidized & reduced zones and decrease in redox potential. Ø Increase in pH of acid soils and a decrease in pH of sodic & calcareous soils. Ø Reduction of ferric (Fe+3) to Ferrous (Fe+2) and Mn+4 to Mn+2 Ø Reduction of NO and NO to N and N O 3 2 2 2 Ø Reduction of SO -2 to SO 2 i.e. extremely reduced conditions 4 2

Ø Increase in the supply of availability of N Ø Increase in the availability of P, Si & Mo Ø Decrease in the concentration of water soluble Zn & Cu Ø Generation of Co , Methane (CH ) & toxic reduction products 2 4 such as organic acids and H S. 2

Inputs for puddled transplanting rice Seed rate: 25 kg/acre or 62.5 kg/ha Spacing: 20 cm x 10 cm No. of seedlings/hill: 2-3 seedlings/hill for 25-30 days aged seedlings 4-5 seedlings/hill for 35 days aged seedlings Optimum population: 50 hills/m2 area Nutrients: 100:50:50 kg NPK ha-1

Transplanting Ø Transplanting of healthy seedlings may be done at 4-5 leaf stage or when they are about 20-25 cm in height @ 2-3 seedlings not deeper than 2-4 cm. Ø Transplanting can be done in two ways. 1. Random transplanting 2. Straight row planting

Advantages of transplanting 1. A good levelling of the field is ensured. 2. Weeds are buried at the time of puddling and weed problem is reduced. 3. The plant population becomes more uniform. 4. The availability of most plant nutrients like P, Fe & K is increased and N is converted better. 5. Seedlings transplanted in soft puddle are able to establish themselves faster and start early tillering and growth. 6. Community nurseries facilitate timely transplanting. 7. The treatment of seedlings for nutrient deficiency and for plant protection against pests and diseases is facilitated before transplanting.

Disadvantages of transplanting 1. It involves extra cost on seed bed preparation, plant protection, pulling and transplanting. 2. It needs higher amount of labour at a time when labour is in short supply. 3. It requires more quantity of water. 4. Seedlings are exposed to possible injury during handling. 5. Plants tend to grow more slowly than direct seeding because of recovery time after transplanting. 6. Harvesting is delayed.

Nutrient management Ø Recommended dosage: 100:50:50 kg NPK ha-1 Ø Time of application: a. Basal dose: 50: 50:50 kg NPK ha-1 b. Split dose: N should be applied in two stages i)Tillering stage – 25 kg N ha-1 ii) Panicle initiation stage – 25 kg ha-1

Source of nutrients: a. FYM b. Green manure c. Azolla d. Biofertilizers e. Inorganic fertilizers (includes macro & micro nutrients) Ø Application of both organic and inorganic manures in combination found to be beneficial in improving the yield and soil fertility status in rice crop.

Ø FYM + Inorganic fertilizers: Ø 10 tons of FYM ha-1 + 50:25:25 kg NPK ha-1 Ø Well decomposed FYM should be applied one week prior to transplanting and should be incorporated in to the soil. Ø Green manuring + Inorganic fertilizers: Ø 5 tons of green manure ha-1 + 50:25:25 kg NPK ha-1 Ø To obtain 5 ton biomass of green manure, we have to broadcast 25 kg seeds of green manure crop viz., sunhemp or dhaincha per hectare Ø Green manure crop should be incorporated to the soil at 45-60 days after sowing or at flowering stage, 2 weeks before transplanting.

Method of application: Broadcast manually Type of nitrogen fertilizer suitable: Ø Puddling results in the conversion of the root zone of the soil from aerobic to anaerobic environment due to depletion of oxygen in the soil profile. The puddled soils develops two zones a. Oxidised zone: It is the upper zone (1 – 10 mm thick) receives oxygen periodically from supply of irrigation water. b. Reduced zone: It is the lower portion without oxygen.

Ø There are two types of nitrogen fertilizers 1. Ammonical nitrogen fertilizers: Urea, Ammonium sulphate. 2. Nitrate nitrogen fertilizer: Calcium ammonium nitrate (CAN) Ammonium sulphate nitrate (ASN) Ø Ammonical form of fertilizers contain more nitrogen Ø Less hygroscopic in nature Ø Not readily available to the crops Ø Takes more time for conversion in to nitrate form

Place of application of nitrogen fertilizers: Ø When ammonical nitrogen fertilizers are applied to the paddy field, gets oxidised to nitrate form (NO -) in the oxidised zone. 3 Ø This nitrate nitrogen in turn leaches down to the reduced zone and gets denitrified to gaseous nitrogen. Ø This loss of nitrogen can be prevented by incorporating ammonical nitrogen in to the reduced zone of the soil before final puddling at 5 cm depth.

Ø The fertilizer containing nitrate such as CAN, ASN are more susceptible to loss of nitrogen through leaching and denitrification compared to ammonical form of nitrogen fertilizers containing no nitrate. Ø The use of nitrate fertilizers should therefore be avoided in paddy.

Why ammonical nitrogen fertilizers are more suited for paddy cultivation? Ø Rice is the only crop which can utilize the ammonical nitrogen. Ø They are less readily available to plants than nitrate fertilizers. The ammonical nitrogen has to nitrify in the soil and be converted into nitrate before it can be taken up by plants. Ø The ammonia in ammonium sulphate is fixed (adsorbed) by the soil immediately after application and it is not leached away like nitrates. Ø Hence, this group of fertilizers may be used in basal application and top dressing.

How to reduce nitrogen loss in Rice? Ø The efficiency of applied nitrogen in paddy soils is nearly 40%. Ø Rest of the applied nitrogen is lost mainly through leaching and denitrification. Ø These losses can be reduced by (1) Delaying the nitrification process of nitrogen fertilizer by altering its granule size. (2) Coating or treating of N fertilizer with different materials. These are called as slow releasing nitrogen fertilizers

1. Use of pre-incubated urea: Ø Mix urea with moist soil at the rate of 1 kg urea with 5 kg soil. Allow this mixture to stand in shade for 36-48 hours before applying in the field. 2. Use of Mud balls: Ø Prepare small balls of moist soil and putting urea or any other fertilisers in the centre of the ball. Ø These balls can be used in the paddy fields where it is not possible to drain out the water from the field at the time of fertilizer application in standing crop

3. Use of neemseed cake: Ø Finely grounded neem seed cake is mixed with urea at the rate of 15-20 per cent. Ø These oil cakes delay nitrate formation from urea and thus reduces the denitrification and leaching. 3. Use of sulphur coated urea granules 4. Use of bigger urea granules. 5. Use of neem coated urea

Efficient management of N fertilizers in wetland rice 1. Proper puddling and levelling to reduce percolation loss of water and nutrients. 2. Apply right quantity at right time (i.e. split application) by right N fertilizers. 3. Deep placement of N fertilizer in reduced soils. 4. Use of slow release N or controlled release of N fertilizer. 5. Combining the concept of slow release and deep placement of N fertilizers. 6. Integrated use of organic manures (including green manures) and bio- fertilisers along with fertilizers 7. By following proper water management practices

Khaira Disease in rice (Zn deficiency) Ø Zinc deficiency is the most common deficiency in wetland rice soils, next to nitrogen and phosphate deficiencies. Reasons for Zn deficiency in lowland rice Ø High pH (>7.0) Ø Prolonged submergence and low redox potential Ø High organic matter and bicarbonate content (HCO ) 3 Ø High Mg : calcium ratio (absorption of Zn as MgCO & CaCO ) 3 3 Ø High available P Ø decreased Zn uptake because of an increase in Iron (Fe), Ca, Mg, Copper (Cu), Manganese (Mn), and P after flooding.

Ø The deficiency of Zn is noticed in the rice crop after 2-3 weeks after transplanting. Zn deficiency symptoms: Ø uneven plant growth and poor tillering Ø In the younger leaves especially base become chlorotic. Ø Appearance of brown blotches and streaks on the lower leaves followed by stunted growth . Ø The size of leaf blade is reduced but not leaf sheath Ø white line sometimes appears along the leaf midrib

Management of Khaira disease: Ø Use fertilizers that generate acidity (e.g., replace some urea with ammonium sulfate). Ø Apply organic manure before seeding or transplanting or applied to the nursery seedbed a few days before transplanting. Ø Drain out of water from the field periodically. Ø Soil application of ZnSO @ 8 kg ha-1 once after 3 crops. 4 Ø By dipping the seedlings in 2% suspension of ZnO for 15 minutes before transplanting. Ø Foliar spray of Zn @1% Ø Growing of varieties tolerant to Zn deficiency eg: IR8, 28, 30 & 34.
Zinc Deficiency Shown by Reduced Tillering, Chlorosis in the Leaves, and Reduced Plant Size (Mature Rice Plants Are Only about 50-80 CM High).

Iron deficiency in rice Ø Iron deficiency is more common in upland, high pH and aerobic soil. Ø The main reason for Fe deficiency is low concentration of iron in upland soil, coarse textured soils and lowland soil with very low organic matter content. Ø Soils with the pH of more than 6.5 are likely to be deficient in available sulphur.

Deficiency symptom: Ø Interveinal chlorosis of emerging leaves Ø less dry matter production Ø stunted growth with narrow leaves Control measures: Ø Soil application of FeSO @ 25 kg ha-1 4 Ø Foliar spray of FeSO @ 1-3% solution 4

Iron toxicity Ø Fe toxicity occurs on a wide range of soils, but generally in lowland rice soils with permanent flooding and in acid soils. Ø Iron toxicity is caused by toxic effects of excessive iron uptake due to large concentration of iron in soil solution. Ø Iron toxicity leads to Akiochi disease in rice. Symptom: Ø Tiny brown spots on lower leaves, starting from tip and spread towards the base of the leaf, and leaves turn from yellow to orange brown and die. Ø Root starts rotting and turns in to black color.

Management of Iron Toxicity: Ø Incorporate lime in the topsoil to raise pH in acid soils Ø Apply additional K, Phosphorus, and Magnesium fertilizers Ø Incorporate about 100−200 kg MnO ha-1 in the topsoil to decrease 2 Fe3+ reduction. Ø Carry out midseason drainage to remove accumulated Fe2+ at the mid- tillering stage (25−30 days after planting/sowing) Ø Drain the field and keep it free of floodwater (but moist) for about 7−10 days to improve oxygen supply during tillering

Water Management Ø The water requirement of rice is not same throughout the crop period. Ø It requires small quantities of water in the early stages, gradually increases its water requirement at flowering and early maturing stage and then decreases to the lowest at later stages of crop growth. Ø Hence, scheduling irrigation to meet the crop water demands at different stages is very important.

Ø The water requirement of the rice crop varies from 150-250 cm. Ø To produce one kg of rice on an average 5000 litre of water is required Ø Water requirement depends on - soil - climate, - season and - variety. Ø The critical stages of rice crop for irrigation is 1. Tillering 2. Panicle initiation 3. Booting 4. Flowering 5. Milking stage

Depth of water to be maintained: Ø Transplanting to panicle initiation stage 2-3 cm depth Ø Panicle initiation to milking stage 5 cm depth Ø Water from the rice field should be drain out once crop reaches dough stage. Mid season drainage Ø Drainage for a period of 5 to 7 days during the beginning of maximum tillering stage. Ø This helps to stimulate the vigorous growth of roots and checks the development of non effective tillers by supplying oxygen in to root system.

Ø Moisture stress at active tillering phase - 30% yield reduction Ø Moisture stress at reproductive phase - 50 - 60% yield reduction Management of percolation losses in rice fields This can be reduced by 1. Growing rice on clayey soil 2. Scrupulous land levelling 3. Thorough puddling 4. Shallow depth of submergence 5. Sub soil compaction Ø Percolation rate of 5mm/day is found to be favourable to for supply of dissolve oxygen , removal of harmful substances and maintenance of root activity

Weed management in transplanted puddled rice Ø The critical period of crop weed competition in rice is up to 15-45 days after transplanting. Ø Competition of weeds in transplanted rice causes 20-30% yield reduction. Ø Integrated weed management approach is found to be better in transplanted puddled rice.
ØThe major weed flora in transplanted puddled rice are categorised in to mono cots, dicots and sedges Echinochloa colona Echinochloa crussgalli Cyperus irria Cyperus difformis

Integrated weed management 1. Cultural Methods: a. Following good crop husbandry practices like Ø good land preparation Ø seed bed preparation Ø method of sowing Ø Spacing 2. Puddling of soil during transplanting to control cynadon and cyperus 3. Flooding of rice fields during crop growth period will reduces the germination of weed seeds. 4. Manual hand weeding at 20 and 50 days after transplanting

II. Chemical method: it includes application of pre and post emergence application of herbicides Pre-emergent herbicides: 2-3 days after transplanting 1. Butachlor 5% g @12 kg acre-1 2. Butachlor 50%EC @ 0.8 lt per acre (mixing with 30 kg sand and should be applied to main field) 3. Anilophos 30% EC @ 0.5 litre in 200 litre of water per acre (if intensity of Echinochloa is more) 4. Pyrazosulfuran ethyl 10% WP @ 100 g per acre 5. Londax power: Bensulfuron methyl (0.6g) + pretilachlor (0.6% g) @ 4 kg per acre

Post emergent herbicides: 3-4 leaf stage of weeds (15-20 DAT) Ø 2,4-D 80% WP @ 1 kg in 200 lt of water per acre Ø Propanil 35% EC @ 3 litre in 200 lt of water per acre Ø Bispysibac sodium 10% SC @ 100 ml in 200 lt of water per acre Ø Bispyribac sodium is a contact herbicides applied as a post emergent herbicide. It has to be applied completely on the foliage of the weeds properly or else its efficiency will be reduced

Introduction Ø System of Rice Intensification (SRI) is special method of rice cultivation originally developed at Madagascar in 1983. Ø It was not known outside Madagaskar till 1997. In 2000 it is introduced in India. Ø In SRI method, fundamental cultivation practices remain more or less same but there is a changes in agronomic practices viz., nursery management, time of transplanting and management of water, nutrients and weeds.

Why System of Rice Intensification? Ø Depletion of water resources. Ø Stagnating rice productivity. Ø Increased importance of organic agriculture. Ø Increasing production costs. Ø Need best utilization of family labour for small and marginal farmers.
6 basic principles of SRI 1. Young-aged seedlings 2. Careful single seedling transplanting 3. Wider spacing 4. Water management 5. Weeding 6. Compost/organic manuring.

Nursery Management 1. Field Nursery: Ø For raising seedlings for one acre 40 m2 area is required. Ø 40 m2 area is divided in to 4 seed bed, each seed bed with the dimension of 1 m width x 10 m length.
Ø On each seed bed, 2 to 3 cm depth of well decomposed FYM should be applied uniformly.
Ø For raising seedling for one acre area, 2 kg seed is required. Ø For each seed bed, 500 g of seeds are distributed uniformly.

Ø After seeds are sown in the seed bed, again 2-3 cm of FYM should be spread on the seed bed. Ø Later each seed bed should be covered with paddy straw and should be irrigated with rose cans 2 times in a day for 5- 6 days to maintain optimum soil moisture condition.
Ø After 4-5 days, paddy straw should be removed from the seed bed and gentle irrigation should be given.
Ø After 12 days, healthy seedlings are ready for transplanting from seed bed.

2. Tray nursery: Ø If farmers found any difficulty for raising seedling in field condition, then they can grow seedling in trays. Ø For raising seedlings for one acre area, 20-25 trays are needed. Ø The dimension of each tray is 50 cm x 20 cm. Ø Foe each trays, 80 g of seeds should be sown.

Land preparation Ø At the early stage of land preparation, deep ploughing should be done once, to loosen the soil and to remove weeds. Ø Then harrowing should be done for 2-3 times for levelling and to break clods. Ø Puddling should be done finally in the presence of water.
Ø After final puddling and before transplanting, 30 cm irrigation channel should be open for every 2 m width in the main field.
Then, 25 cm x 25 cm or 30 cm x 30 cm square marking should be done in the main field by using Iron rake or by wooden marker.
Ø 12 days old seedlings from the seed bed should be uprooted very carefully in such a way that, each seedling should be in contact with seed, roots and soil.

Ø After seedling uprooting, only one seedling should be transplanted in each hill very care fully with out damaging the seed, roots and soil. Ø Soil should be at saturated condition at transplanting (no standing water)

Nutrient Management RDF : 100-50-50 kg NPK ha-1 Ø 10 t of FYM or 5 t of green manure should be applied 2-3 week before transplanting. Ø At the time of transplanting, 50 % recommended N & K and full dose of P should be applied as basal dose. Ø The remaining 25% of N should be applied at 30 DAT (at tillering stage). Ø The remaining 25% N and 50% of K should be applied at 60 DAT (at panicle initiation stage).

Weed management Ø The critical period of crop weed competition is 15-45 DAT. Ø Since moisture is maintained at saturation condition throughout the crop growth period, intensity of weed for natural resource competition is more. Ø As compared to chemical method of weed control, weeding with manually or machine operated cono-rotary weedor is found to be more superior and advantageous in SRI method of rice cultivation.
Ø Weeding should be done by using cono-rotary weeder for five times i.e. 12, 24, 36, 48 and 60 DAT.

Advantages of cono-rotary weedor in SRI Ø Weeding with cono-weedor helps in aeration, which helps in increasing root biomass and more nutrient and water uptake, which results in production of more number of tillers/hill (30-50 tillers/hill). Ø No. of productive tillers is more in SRI method as compared to puddled transplanted rice. Ø In puddled transplanted rice cultivation decaying of roots takes place after 50 DAT, which leads to lesser number of productive tillers and decreases water and nutrient uptake leading to lower test weight and more chaffy grains.

Pre-emergent herbicide: (3-5 DAT) Ø Londax power: Bensulfuron methyl (0.6g) + pretilachlor (0.6% g) @ 4 kg per acre Post emergent herbicide: (20 DAT) Ø Bispysibac sodium 10% SC @ 100 ml in 200 lt of water per acre

Water Management Ø After transplanting, field should be irrigated very lightly (maintain saturation point) for every 2-3 days throughout the crop growth period. Ø Moisture should be maintained in such a way that there should not be any hair line cracks in the soil and also their should not be stagnation of water in the field. Ø Alternate wetting and drying should be followed. Ø In this way, we can able to save 45-50% of water.
point Moisture should be maintained at saturation throughout crop growth stage

Plant Protection Ø Incidence of pest and diseases in SRI method of rice cultivation is very less as compared to puddled transplanted method of rice cultivation. Ø If any pest and diseases is found to be beyond economic threshold level suitable plant protection measure should be taken as per the suitable recommendations.

Harvesting and Yield Ø In SRI method of rice cultivation, crop will mature 10 days early as compared to transplanted puddled rice. Ø In SRI method of rice cultivation, their will be increase in the yield up to 15-20% as compared to puddled transplanted rice.

SRI: Ø12 days old seedlings are transplanted | Puddled Transplanting: Ø25-30 days old seedlings are transplanted
SRI: ØSingle seedlings are transplanted/hill | Puddled Transplanting: Ø3-4 seedlings are transplanted/hill
SRI: ØInter and intra row spacing is followed (25x25cm) | Puddled Transplanting: ØProper spacing is not followed
SRI: ØMore application of organic manures | Puddled Transplanting: ØLess application of organic manures
SRI: ØWater is maintained at saturation point | Puddled Transplanting: Ø5 cm height of water is allowed to stand
SRI: ØMore no. of tillers and productive tillers/hill | Puddled Transplanting: ØLess no. of tillers and productive tillers/hill

Advantages of SRI method of rice cultivation Ø Higher grain yield and straw yield (15-20%) Ø Reduction in crop duration by 10 days Ø Lesser seed rate (2 kg/acre) Ø Savings in water requirement up to 45-50% Ø More no. of productive tillers Ø More use of organic manures Ø Lesser chaffy grains Ø Improvement in soil health through biological activity Ø Reduction in methane emission

In DSR 2 types of transplanting 1. Direct seeded rice in wet condition: Drum Seeding Rice Ø Puddling is followed Ø Seedlings are not raised in nursery Ø Pre-germinated seeds are directly sown in the field using seed drill. Ø All the other agronomic practices remain similar as that of transplanted puddled rice cultivation.

Advantages of DSR: Ø This method is popularly adopted in the areas of acute labour shortage for transplanting. Ø Puddling and transplanting can be completed in a single day without wasting time for nursery. Ø Timely sowing is possible Ø Crop matures 10 days earlier as compared to transplanted rice. Ø 10-15 per cent water can be saved. Ø Rice yield can be increased by 5-10%.

Inputs: Ø Seed rate – 25-30 kg/ ha. Ø Seeds should be soaked in water for 24 hr. Ø The pre soaked seeds should be treated with carbendazim @ 4g/ kg seed. Ø The treated seed should be filled in wet gunny bag, tied loosely and maintained in warm condition for 24 hr. Ø Then the pre-germinated seeds should be filled in four drums of the drum seeder.

Land preparation: Ø Puddling should be done and excess water should be removed and maintained soft muddy layer. Water management: Ø up to 10 days after seeding, water should not be stagnated and it should not dry. Soil should be maintained at saturation point. Stagnation of water immediately after sowing leads to rotting of seeds. Ø After 15 days, as like in the puddled transplanted rice, water should be maintained at 2cm depth up to tillering stage and after tillering depth should be increased up to 5 cm.

Weed management: Ø Weeds compete with rice seedlings in the very early stage of the crop growth and reduces the yield subsequently. Ø It is necessary to go for 2 hand weeding at 20 days and 40 days after sowing. Ø Application of pre-emergent herbicide at 3-5 DAS and post emergent herbicide at 15-20 DAS is found to be promising.

2. Direct seeded rice in dry condition: Aerobic rice cultivation Ø Dry seeds are directly dibbled in the rows. Ø Puddling is not followed Ø No need of raising nursery beds Ø Irrigation is provided once in 3-5 days to maintain moisture at field capacity.

Ø If rice grown under dry condition with assured irrigation is called as aerobic rice cultivation. Ø If rice grown under dry condition without assured irrigation and completely depended on rainfall, it is called as Rainfed upland rice cultivation.

Cultivation aspects of Aerobic rice Land preparation: Ø Land is ploughed 2 to 3 times, clods were broken and levelled using harrow and soil should be in fine tilth condition. Inputs: Ø FYM: 10 t/ha. Ø Seed rate: 8-10 kg/ha. Ø Fertilizers: 100:50:50 kg NPK/ha.

Sowing: Ø Dry seeds are dibbled in a row spacing of 25 cm or 30 cm. Ø Line sowing could also be done using seed drill. Ø After sowing, land should be irrigated uniformly to ensure enough soil moisture during germination.

Varieties/ Hybrids: Ø All the varieties and hybrids growing under puddled transplanted condition are suitable for growing under aerobic condition. Ø Aerobic rice varieties: MAS 946-1, MAS-26. Season of sowing: Ø Aerobic rice can be sown up to end of July for obtaining optimum yield. Ø If sowing is done after first fort night of august, the panicle initiation stage is coincide with the low temperature during November and December, which affect the heading, flowering and pollination of the crop and resulted in poor yield because of more chaffy grains.

Water management: Ø In aerobic rice cultivation, crop can be irrigated through surface irrigation or through drip. Ø If surface irrigation is followed, crop should be irrigated once in 3-4 days to maintain soil moisture at field capacity. Ø If irrigation is scheduled through drip, crop should be irrigate once in two days for a period of 2-3 hours.

Nutrient management: Ø 10 t of FYM is applied 3 weeks prior to sowing. Ø 50 % recommended N and full dose of P & K should be applied in the rows and should be mix properly before dibbling of seed. Ø Remaining 50% of N should be applied at tillering and panicle initiation stage. Micronutrient management: Ø In aerobic rice cultivation deficiency of Zn and Fe is more common. Ø Soil application of ZnSO @ 8 kg/acre. 4 Ø Foliar spray of Fe(SO4) at 0.5%. 2

Weed Management: Ø Weed infestation is seviour during early stage of the crop in aerobic situation. Ø Passing of cono-rotary weeders could be used to control weeds apart from loosening the soil in initial stage of the crop. Pre-emergent: • Pyrazosulfuron ethyl (10%) @ 1 g per litre of water. • Londax power @ 10 kg/ha @ 2-3 days after sowing. Post emergent: • Byspiribac sodium (10%) @0.08 litre/ha at 15-20 DAS.

Advantages of aerobic rice: Ø 10-15% higher grain yield due to more number of tillers per hill (>50) Ø 55-60% water saving Ø Increased water productivity Ø Decreased consumption of inputs like water, nutrients, energy and labour Ø Less or no impact on environment by reduced methane emission.
Targeted areas of Aerobic rice: Ø Uplands Ø Undulating rainfed lowlands Ø Water short irrigated lowlands.
Rice production in saline and sodic soils Saline soils: pH – 7.5 to 8.5 ESP - < 15% Sodic soils: pH - > 8.5 ESP - > 15% (dominated with sodium carbonate and sodium bi-carbonates)

Management of saline and sodic soils 1. Soil management: Ø Providing proper drainage Ø Application of FYM or growing of green manure crops and incorporation in to soil Ø Application of Gypsum (CaSo ) based on soil test value 2 weeks prior 4 to transplanting. Ø Application of 25% extra recommended dose of nitrogen and phosphorous. (Ammonical N fertilizers are preferred) Ø Soil application of ZnSO @ 8 kg/acre 4

2. Crop Management: Ø Planting of 30-35 days age old seedlings Ø Planting of 5-6 seedlings/hill Ø Planting at closer spacing 15 cm x 10 cm to maintained optimum plant population. Ø Use of saline tolerant rice varieties: Prakash, Rashi, Mangala, Vikas and IR-30864

3. Water management: Ø Flooding the land with fresh water once in 15 days and providing proper drainage. Ø Providing proper drainage all along the field for leaching out the excess salts from the field.

Dr. M. Mahadevappa, Ø popularly known as Rice Mahadevappa is an Indian Agricultural Scientist and Plant Breedor, renowned for developing high yielding hybrid varieties of rice. Harvesting of rice: Ø Turning the crop colour from green to yellow is the general symptom of maturity. Ø At this stage, the grain starts maturing from top to bottom of the panicle. Ø About a week prior to harvest of the crop, the water is let out from the field completely.

Ø For shattering varieties, crop should be harvested before panicle is fully dried. Ø At the time of harvest, some of the grains at the base of the earhead will be green. If it is fully riped, the rice gets broken during milling.

Ø Harvesting of rice is done either manually or through combined harvester. Yield: Ø It varies from season to season, and variety to variety besides several other factors. While the average yields vary from 4-5 tons/ha for varieties and 8-10 t/ha for hybrids during kharif. Ø A minimum of 1 more tonne can be expected during rabi for HYV.

Processing of rice Ø Processing of rice usually involves milling and polishing. Ø Milling: The outermost layer of rice called the hull is removed to make brown rice. Brown rice is rice with the whole kernel intact is still surrounded by all layers of bran. Ø Polishing: removal of aleurone layer that remains on the rice. This step is called polishing. Polished rice is called as White rice. Ø The bran, germ, and aleurone layers of rice contain most of the fat content found in rice and are the source of fat-soluble vitamins like vitamin E as well as many other nutrients.

Hulling/ milling percentage: Hulling % = (weight of rice / weight of paddy grains) x 100 Ø Hulling percentage in rice is 65-75% By products of rice: 1. Husk: used as cheap fuel and bedding in poultry houses under deep litter system. 2. Rice bran: contains 12- 14% rice bran oil (Branola) prescribed for heart patients.

PARBOILING Ø A hydrothermal treatment of rice grain immediately after drying prior to milling to prepare parboiled grains is called parboiling. Ø The soaking of a rice grain in hot water results in swelling of the starch granules. Ø Soaking in hot water weakens the granule structure by breaking the hydrogen bond which consequently provides a larger surface for the absorption of water by the starch granules. The whole process is called gelatinization. Ø Later on, moist heating is done to provide the irreversible swelling or the fusion of the starch granules. Ø Steam is used for moist heating called steam rice.

1. Raw paddy rice 2. Vitamins and minerals 3. Soaking in warm water, in the bran. the nutrients become more soluble and move out of the bran. 4. To move these nutrients 5. Parboiled rice carries into the kernel, hot steam 80% of the nutrients and air pressure are used, of brown rice. otherwise they would rinse out into the water.

Advantages of parboiling Ø The percentage of broken grains is reduced Ø More nutritious than raw rice Ø Renders more resistant to insects during storage. Ø Loss of solids in gruel is less than raw rice during cooking. Ø The bran from parboiled rice contains higher oil content.

Disadvantages Ø Parboiled rice takes more time to cook. Ø Common rice consumer may not like the flavour and colour of the par boiled rice. Ø Parboiled rice may contain higher moisture content and some mycotoxins may develop. Ø The milling cost of parboiled rice is higher since the shelled grains are comparatively harder.

YIELD & YIELD ESTIMATES OF RICE Ø Yield of rice in a given field condition can be estimated by the following parameters 1. No. of panicles/m2 2. Average no. of grains per panicle 3. Percentage of filled grains 4. Weight of the grain (test weight) (Yield/m2 = 1 x 2 x 3 x 4)

Reasons for low yield in rice Ø Widely varying climatic conditions under which rice is grown. Ø Inefficient utilization of applied N. Ø Limited scope for optimum water management in heavy rainfall areas. Ø Cloudiness and its ill effects on the photosynthetic activity of rice in monsoon (80% of the season is cloudy during kharif) Ø Adverse effects of soil salinity or alkalinity

Ø Susceptibility to heavy incidence of pests and diseases which tend to increase under ideal crop conditions. Ø Little scope for rainfed upland rice to achieve its yield potential fully due to short growing season and practically no control over time of transplantation in assured rainfall areas without irrigation facilities. Ø Indiscriminate use of fertilizers. Ø Monoculture rice farming Ø Poor drainage

Measures to improve the yield Ø Tailoring new varieties which can effectively photosynthesize even under low light intensity. Eg : IET 9354, Vijaya. Ø Integrated pest and disease management practices Ø Growing varieties tolerant to salinity and drought. Eg: Prakash, mangala, vijaya. Ø Increasing cropping intensity through early maturing modern rice varieties. Ø Adopting best agronomical practices like adjusting the date of planting in a given locality in such a way that the last 6 weeks of a variety pass through cloud free days. Ø Practicing integrated weed and nutrient management practices.
Bio-fertilizer application Ø The bio-fertilizer suitable for rice cultivation is Azospirillum. Ø Azospirillum can be applied in three forms 1. Seed treatment 2. Soil application 3. Root treatment

I. Seed treatment (Direct seed rice): 1. 50 g of Jaggery should be mixed in 500 ml of water and the mixture should be boiled for 5-10 min. 2. Jaggery solution should be sprinkled on the 25 kg of the seed, later 400 g of Azospirillum should be mixed. 3. The treated seed should be dried in shade for 30 min.
II. Soil Application: Ø 800 g of Azospirillum should be mixed with 10 kg of well decomposed FYM and 10 kg of Soil and applied to the field.

III. Root treatment: Ø 6 ft length and 6 ft width of bed should be prepared and 4 inch of water should be allowed to stand. Ø In this area, 400 g of Azospirillum is mixed with water and seedlings are immersed in the bed for 10-15 minutes before transplanting.

Role of silicon nutrition in Rice Ø Rice is a high silicon accumulating plant. Ø Si is a beneficial element for plant growth and not a essential element but it is agronomically essential for improving and sustaining rice productivity. Ø Silicon is absorbed as monosilicic acid by rice plants in larger quantities than the macronutrients, for example, silicon uptake is 108% greater than Nitrogen (N) uptake. Ø A rice crop producing a yield of 5000 kg.ha-1 removes 230-470 kg Si ha -1.

Ø Si increases the mechanical strength of the stem, thus reducing crop lodging. Ø Besides rice yield increase, Si has many fold advantages of increasing nutrient availability (N, P, K, Ca, Mg, S, Zn). Ø It decreases the nutrient toxicity (Fe, Mn, P, Al) and minimizing biotic and abiotic stress in plants. Ø It reduces oxidative stress and it help in alleviating salt damage. Ø It will reduces the incidence of occurrence of blast disease in rice plant. Ø It reduces the insect attack in rice crop.

Silicon deficiency leads to: 1. Soft and droopy leaves which cause lodging and mutual shading. 2. Reduced photosynthetic activity. 3. Reduced grain yields. 4. Increased occurrence of diseases such as blast. 5. Reduced number of panicles and filled spikelet's per panicle

Ø Silicon deficiency is not very common in irrigated rice. Ø It occurs in areas with poor soil fertility, and is common in old and degraded paddy soils. Ø It also occurs in organic soils with small mineral Si reserves, and in highly weathered and leached tropical soils in the rainfed lowland and upland areas. Management: Ø recycling of rice straw (5−6% Si) and rice husks (10% Si). Ø Application of Ca silicate: 120–200 kg/ha; K silicate: 40–60 kg/ha for rapid correction. Ø Foliar spray of Si @0.1-0.2% with sodium silicate improve Si nutrition.

Ø Maize is one of the important cereal crops in the world’s agricultural economy both as food for men and feed for animals, because of its higher yield potential compared to other cereals. Hence it is called as “Queen of Cereals”.

Classification of maize Ø Classification is mainly based on the character of the kernels and mainly related to type of starch (hard v/s soft) in grains. Ø It is classified in to 7 groups 1. Flint corn – Zea mays indurata (all hard) Ø Starchy endosperm enclosed with hard kernal. Ø Kernel size is large with flat bottom and round at the top. Ø High proportion of starch. Ø Colour may be white or yellow. Ø This is the type mostly grown in India.

2. Dent corn – Zea mays indentata (Soft centre) Ø Kernels is having both hard and soft starches. Ø Soft starches is in the centre of kernel but hard starch extends on the sides. Ø Depression or dent in the crown on the seed is the result of drying and shrinkage of soft starch. Ø This type is widely grown in USA
3. Pop corn – Zea mays averta (core of soft) Ø Kernel size is small. Ø Presence of soft endosperm at the core of the seed.

4. Sweet corn – Zea mays Saccharata Ø The sugar and starch make the major components of the endosperm that results in sweet taste of kernels. Ø It is mainly grown in USA. Ø The cobs are picked up green for canning and table purpose.

5. Flour corn – Zea mays amylaceae (all soft) Ø The grain appears flint corn. Ø The grains are composed of soft starch and have little or no dent are called as “Soft Corn”. Ø It is widely grown in USA and South Africa.
6. Pod corn – Zea mays tunicata (husk like glumes) Ø Each kernel is enclosed in a pod or husk in an ear.

7. Waxy corn – Zea mays cerabina Ø The kernel looks to have waxy appearance and gummy starch in them, because of amylopectin. Ø The starch is similar to that of Tapioca starch for making adhesive for articles.
Origin of Maize Ø Mexico and Central America. CIMMYT: International Centre for the Improvement of Maize and Wheat. Ø It is located at Mexico.

Economic importance and uses Ø Most important cereal crop in the world’s agriculture economy. 85% is consumed as human food. Ø Green cobs are roasted and eaten by the people. Ø Corn has low fibre content, more carbohydrate and most palatable. Ø Widely used in preparation of cattle feed and poultry feed. Ø It can be used as a green fodder. It has no HCN content. Ø Can be preserved as silage. Ø Food products: Corn meal, corn flakes.

Ø Industrial products: Alcohol, Corn Starch (Dextrose), glucose, corn oil, corn syrup. Ø Used in canning industry, production of polymer, making paper. Ø Maize grain contains Protein – 10% Oil – 4% Crude fibre – 2.3% Carbohydrate – 70% Albuminoides – 10.4%

Ø Maize protein “Zein” is deficit in two amino acids viz., Lysine and Tryptophan. Ø Maize has a significant quantity of Vitamin – A, nicotinic acid, riboflavin and Vitamin E. Ø Maize is low in Calcium but fairly high in “P”.

Climatic requirements Ø It is essentially a tropical crop. Ø It is a C short day plant. 4 Ø Though it is a tropical crop, it has got high adaptability to wider climate 550 N to 450 S. Ø It can be grown up to 2500 m above MSL. Ø Maize requires moist and warm weather from germination to flowering. Ø Optimum temperature for germination is 210 C and for growth is 320 C. Ø 500-750 mm rainfall with well distributed is ideal for proper growth.

Ø Extremely high temperature and low RH at flowering, desiccate the pollen resulting in poor pollen grain formation. Ø Temp. > 350 C reduces the pollen germination and temp < 150 C delays silking and tasseling.

Soil Requirements Ø Maize is best adapted to well drained sandy loam to silt loam soil. Ø Maize can not thrive on heavy soil, especially on low lands. Ø Water stagnation is extremely harmful to the crop, therefore proper drainage is must. Ø The alluvial soils of UP, Bihar and Punjab are very suitable for growing maize crop. Ø pH ranges from 5.5 to 7.5. Ø Salinity and water logging are harmful at seeding stage. Ø Continuous water logging for 3 days reduces the yield by 40-45%.

Water Management Ø Maize is very susceptible to excess water and moisture stress. Ø Water stagnation for 3 days will spoil the entire crop. Ø Maize can tolerate heavy rains provided water does not stand in the field for long periods. Therefore proper drainage is essential. Ø 500-600mm of water is required during its lifecycle. Ø At this stage water shortage for 2 days reduce yield by 20%. If it is for 6-8 days yields are reduced by 50%.

Weed management Ø Crop weed competition in maize is up to 25-30 DAS. Ø After 30 DAS weeds will be suppressed due to shading effect of the main crop. Hence, it is necessary to control weeds till 25-30 days. Ø Inter cultivation is done in between rows at 15 and 30 DAS with small implements i.e., small blade harrow - i) to remove weeds ii) to stir/loose the top soil and iii) to give slight earthing up to maize plants Ø Pre-emergent application of Atrazine 50 % WP @ 1-1.25 kg a.i./ha (Sole crop) Ø Pendimethalin 30% EC @ 1 kg a.i./ha (Intercrop) followed by one hand weeding at 30 DAS. Classification of wheat  Wheat is classified in to three groups based on their chromosomes number. 1. Diploid wheat: 2n=14 T. monococcum (Einkorn) 2. Tetraploid wheat: 2n=28 T. durum (durum/ marconi wheat) T. dicoccum (Emmer wheat) 3. Hexaploid wheat: 2n=42 T. aestivum (Bread wheat) T. spelta (spelt wheat) T. vulgare

II. Wheat is also classified based on season of cultivation 1. Winter wheat: Which requires a low temperature of 0 – 8o c during transition from vegetative to reproductive phase.  These type of wheat should requires 30-60 days of chilling temperature.  These wheat are grown during September to November in Northern hemisphere and harvested in early summer.  These type of wheat is predominantly grown in USA.

2. Spring wheat: Which do not requires low temperatures during transition from vegetative to reproductive phase (3-15o C).  This type of wheat is grown during Late November/ December and harvested at late summer (April-May).  South Asia (India, Pakistan, Nepal, Bangladesh), North Africa, the Middle East and the lower latitudes (e.g. Sonora in Mexico).

Origin of Wheat  Tetraploid wheat originated about 8000 years back between Syria and Iraq but,  T. durum is domesticated in Central Europe  T. dicoccum was domesticated in South eastern Iraq.  Hexaploid bread wheat was originated in Iran and Afganisthan but domesticated in North Western India.

Soil and climatic condition  Wheat can be grown on widely varying soils with good drainage and moisture holding capacity.  Soils with clay loam with good water holding capacity is ideal.  Heavy soils with poor drainage are not suitable, since wheat is sensitive to water logging.  pH: 5.5-6.5 (can withstand slight acidity & alkalinity). In India wheat growing areas can be mainly divided in to 5 soil types: 1. Gangetic alluvium of UP & Bihar 2. Indus Alluvium of Punjab & Haryana 3. Black soil regions of Central & Southern India comprising MP, MH & Karnataka 4. Hilly regions of the Himalaya 5. Desert soils of Rajasthan

Climatic condition: Latitude:  Wheat is a widely adopted crop grown in tropical, subtropical, temperate and in extreme cold tract beyond 60o N latitude.  It can tolerate severe cold climate.  It is a long day plant requires longer day length for flowering.  Wheat crop takes 180 days in hills of North India ; western region and 100 days in Peninsular India for maturity Rainfall:  It can be grown in annual rainfall region of 300-1130 mm. In India, it is grown in the regions from 100 mm in Rajasthan to the regions of very high rainfall up to 4000 mm in humid Western Plains.

Why area and production of wheat in India is low?  In India, wheat is grown during rabi or winter season.  The high temperatures on both ends of wheat season restrict the cultivation of this crop in India.  Too cooler months, high temperatures in September do not permit good tillering of the crop. They also favour root rot and seedling blight.  Hot summer during the grain ripening period hastens the maturity of the crop giving inferior quality of the crop.

STAGES OF CROP GROWTH 1. CRI: Crown root initiation  CRI takes place 15-21 DAS. Plants at this stage are very sensitive to soil moisture stress. Hence, there is a need for adequate moisture at this stage.
2. TILLERING: The lateral buds at these nodes give rise to tillers. Tiller initiation takes place 4 weeks after sowing and tillers continue to emerge for another 2 or 3 weeks.

3. JOINTING STAGE :  It represents the node production and active growth period.  Upto this stage, the seedlings consists of a whorl of leaves.  At this jointing stage, the stem becomes visible with distinct nodes.

4. HEADING :  This is the stage where the internodes begin to elongate.  Flag leaf and ear emerge towards the end of this stage.  Adequate moisture should also be present in the soil at the heading stage.

5. Flowering and grain development :  After heading, flowering takes place and reaches grain filling stage.  Later it reaches to soft dough stage of the grain.  At this stage also, the plant requires adequate moisture at dough stage.  Awns are attached to Lemma. Green awns are photosynthetically active and contributes 15% of net photosynthesis.  Botanically seed is called as Kernal.

Production Techniques Land preparation:  Land should be ploughed 2-3 times with the help of cultivator to bring soil to fine tilt. Later with the help of harrow field should be levelled properly. Method of sowing: 1. Broad casting 2. Sowing behind the plough with hand 3. Sowing behind the plough with seed drill 4. Dibbling 5. Zero tillage sowing

Spacing:  Irrigated condition: Dibbling 2 or 3 seeds by hand at 4-6 cm depth at a distance of 22.5 cm x 10-15 cm spacing under normal sowing and 15 -18 cm row spacing at late sowing condition.  Rainfed condition: 30 cm row to row Time of sowing:  Optimum sowing time is 15th October to 15th November.  Early sowing with long duration Varieties – sown during october.  For late sowing varieties with less than 100 days – end of November.
Seed Rate  Normal condition: 100 kg ha-1  Late sowing: 125 kg ha-1 Recommended varieties  H.D. 2189  DWR-39 (Keerthi)  DWR-39

Water management:  Adequate soil moisture is required for normal development of the wheat plant at all the stages of growth.  The water require of crop is around 40-45 cm.  The critical stages for irrigation are 1. CRI, 2. tillering, 3. jointing, 4. flowering, 5. milking and 6. dough stage.  Hence, 4-6 irrigation is required for obtaining better yield.

Scheduling of irrigation at normal condition  1irrigation: CRI at 20-25 DAS  2 irrigation: tillering stage at 40-45 DAS  3 irrigation: late jointing stage at 70-75 DAS  4 irrigation: flowering stage at 90-95 DAS  5 irrigation: dough stage at 110-115 DAS Scheduling of irrigation at limited water supply  If only one irrigation: CRI stage  If only 2 irrigation: CRI and flowering stage  If only 3 irrigation: CRI, late jointing (booting) and milking stage.  If only 4 irrigation: CRI, late tillering, late jointing & flowering stage.

Weed management:  Critical period of crop weed competition is up to 35-40 days.  Phalaris minor is a crop associated weed in wheat crop a. Manual weeding at 20 and 40 DAS b. Pre-emergent application of Pendimethalin @ 3.3 l/ha c. Post emergent application: Isoproturon 50% @1.5 kg a.i./ha 2,4-D 36% @1.5 kg a.i./ha at 30-DAS.

Varietal development of Wheat  “Norin” dwarf gene was isolated from Norin series wheat varieties and “Nor”(Rht) in wheat variety in Japan.  Rht – Reduced height.  The first such variety “Norin-10” (dwarf gene wheat) was brought to USA by S.C. Salamon in 1948.

 Using “Norin” genes Dr. O. A. Vogel developed a dwarf winter wheat variety “Grains” in USA and many other varieties were developed by Dr. Norman Borloug, Nobel laureate in 1961-62 at CIMMYT, Mexico.  In 1963, Govt. of India imported 100 kg of Mexican wheat varieties Sonora 63, Sonora 64 and Lerma Rojo 64, with the help of Rockfeller foundation.  After extensive tests, huge quantities of Lerma Rojo 64 A (single gene dwarf variety) and Sonora 64 (Double gene dwarf variety) were imported in 1965-1966 from CIMMYT.

 In 1965 both varieties were released for general cultivation in India and brought green revolution.  Later, these varieties were replaced by Kalyansona and Sonalika. Crop: Sorghum (Great millet) S.N: Sorghum bicolor Family: Poacea

Economic Importance  Sorghum is also called as Jowar/ Jwar/ Cholam/ Jola in India.  In Europe it is called as Guinea Corn.  It is the third important staple food crop of India and Asia and fifth important cereal crop after Rice, Wheat, Maize and Barley.  Millions of people in Africa depend on sorghum as their staple food.  It is a well known drought resistant crop, hence grown in arid and semi arid regions under rainfed condition  It is grown both on marginal and rich lands, with or without irrigation.

 Sorghum grains are well known for their high nutritional values due to their, Low fat (3%), high starch (>70%), high protein (10-12%), rich in Iron (>70 ppm) and Zinc (> 50 ppm), which helps in reducing the micronutrient malnutrition globally.  Sorghum is deficit in Amino acids like Arginine, Glycine, Tyrosine and Methionine.  Sorghum is mainly consumed as roti and popped sorghum (India), fermented beer (Africa), Sweet syrup in condiments/breads/biscuits (USA).  Grains are used as industrial raw material to produce ethanol (biofuel) and to ferment other liquors.

Reasons for drought resistance in sorghum  Slow shoot growth till roots are well developed.  Higher root weight/ volume than most other cereals (well proliferated root system).  Deeper root system than any other cereal crop.  Maintain high turgor pressure during stress by reducing leaf osmotic potential.  Produce large epicuticular waxes on stem and leaves to reduce transpiration.  Roll the leaf surface under stress by special motor cells in leaf tissues.
Origin of Sorghum  East and Central Africa (Ethiopia/ Sudan) is regarded as the place of origin of sorghum.  It reached India at around 1500 BC, while it entered USA as late as 125 years back.

Area and distribution of Sorghum India ranks 3rd in area and production but 4th in productivity The major jowar growing states in India are Maharashtra, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Tamil Nadu ,Gujarat and Uttar Pradesh.

Climatic requirement of Sorghum  It is primarily a tropical warm weather crop but can be grown in sub tropics and temperate regions during warm months.  It is a sturdy/ hardy crop and can withstand varied climatic hazards more than any other cereal crop.  It is successfully grown in arid areas of UP, Rajasthan and also in humid regions of W. Bengal and Bihar.  It can not be grown beyond 400 N and 400 S.  It can withstand wide range of temperatures varying from 15.50 C to 40.50 C with rainfall variations of 35-150 cm per annum.  This crop can be grown from sea level to as high as 1500 m.  Sorghum is a short day plant. Flowering and grain formation starts when day length shortens during winter.

Soil Requirement  Sorghum can be grown in heavy black soils to red soils, but comes up well in heavy black soils.  Jowar does not grow well under sandy and marshy soils.  The crop grows well in neutral pH of 7.0 but it can withstand the pH of 6.0 – 8.5 as it considerably withstand salinity and alkalinity.  During kharif season crop grown under black soils, where as under rabi and summer season crop can be grown under sandy soils with assured irrigation facility.

Land preparation  Deep ploughing should be done to a depth of 20-25 cm to loose the soil.  It should be followed by 2 to 3 ploughing with country plough.  Later harrowing should be done to break the clods and to level the field.

Seeds and Sowing:  Sorghum is sown by various methods in different parts of the country, 1. Broadcasting, 2. Seed drilling 3. Dibbling  For obtaining higher yield, seeds should be sown in lines using seed drill. Seed rate: 12-15 kg ha-1 Spacing: 45 x 15 cm Depth of sowing: 5 cm

Time of sowing  In India, Sorghum is grown in all the three season. 1. Kharif : June –July.  In Northern India, sorghum is sown only in kharif season. Under irrigated condition first week of June is ideal, under rainfed condition, crop should be sown with onset of monsoon.  Timely planted kharif crop escapes the damage of shoot fly and midge. 2. Rabi: Mid-September - mid-October (MH, Karnataka & AP) 3. Summer: January – February (TN, AP & some parts of Karnataka)

Varieties and hybrids Among all the cultivars, CSH-1 hybrid is more suitable for ratoon crop and the local varieties are not at all fit for ratooning. This is only possible under irrigated conditions.

Manures & Fertilizers:  Sorghum requires heavy doses of fertilizers because it removes nutrients in heavy amount from the soil. Manures and fertilizers both play an important role in sorghum cultivation. FYM: 8 t ha-1. NPK: Irrigated:100: 75: 40 kg ha-1 Rainfed: 65: 40: 40 kg ha-1 Basal dose: 50% N & full dose of P & K Split dose: 50% N at 30-35 days.  In rainfed crop, entire quantity should be applied at the time of sowing. Fe deficiency: Sorghum is more sensitive to Fe deficiency (Foliar spray of FeSO4 @ 0.5 -1%) Zn Deficiency: 15-20 kg ha-1 of ZnSO at the time of sowing. 4

Thinning and intercultural operation  To maintain desirable plant population of 1,50,000 ha-1, thinning should be done two times at 10-15 DAS and at 20-25 DAS.  Sorghum is a slow growing crop up to 30-40 DAS, hence there will be more competition from the weeds and also to improve the growth intercultural operation should be carried out to supply aeration to the roots by loosening the soil and formation of earthing up.  Two intercultural operations should be done. First at 20 DAS and second at 45 DAS after split application of N (earthingup).

Water Management  Water requirement of sorghum is 30-35 cm.  Generally it is grown as rainfed crop and drought resistant in nature but responds well to irrigation.  However, in case of no rains, the crop may be irrigated once or twice to a depth of 5 cm, especially in heading and grain development stage.  Whenever the crop is irrigated, it is always useful to adopt the ridges and furrow method.

Critical stages of irrigations are 1. Germination (at the time of sowing) 2. Knee high stage (30-35 DAS) 3. Flag leaf stage (50-55DAS) 4. Flowering (70-75 DAS) 5. Grain formation stage (100-105DAS) Under irrigated condition:  In sandy loam soils irrigation should be given at once in 8 days, where as in clay loam soils irrigation should be given at 15 days once, in general 6 to 8 irrigation is required for successful crop of sorghum.

Weed management  Sorghum is a slow growing crop up to 35-40 DAS.  After 40 DAS weeds will be suppressed due to shading effect of the main crop and also due to allelopathic effect. Hence, it is necessary to control weeds till 40 days.  Inter cultivation is done in between rows with small implements i.e., small blade harrow - i) to remove weeds ii) to stir/loose the top soil and iii) to give slight earthing up to jowar plants  Pre-emergent application of Atrazine 50 % WP @ 0.5-0.75 kg a.i./ha.  Post-emergent application of 2,4-D @ 0.75-1.0 kg a.i./ha at 15-20 DAS

 Striga (Striga asiatica) is a crop associated root parasitic weed in Sorghum and damaging the crop up to 5-90%.  Striga is also called as witch weed which affects Maize, sorghum, Sugarcane and some legume crop.

Management of Striga Weed  Striga infestation is more in low fertile soils. 1. Deep ploughing 2. Growing of Trap Crops like cotton, cowpea, groundnut, sunflower, linseed, field bean, soybean in rotation. These crops stimulate the germination of striga seeds but not parasite leads to suicidal effect. 3. Grow resistant varieties: Secrete stimuli but not parasite, Nadyal, bilichigun, N-13, Co-20, CS- 3541, RS-813 4. Mechanical: Hand pulling and destroying before produce flowers. 5. Chemical: Application of atrazin @ 1 kg ai/ha as pre emergent and 2.4-D @ 1 kg ai/ha as post emergent at 2-3 weeks after sowing. 6. Application of excessive N and FYM 7. Injecting of ethylene @ 3kg/ha in 4-6 inch layer of soil is found to be effective in inducing 80-90% of germination of striga.
