Tripura, Assam, Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. At its appearance, it shows long, elliptical, grayish-green or tan lesions ranging from 2.5 to 15 cm in length on the leaves. For control of TLB, spray Zineb/Meneb @ 2.5-4.0 g/liter of water (2- 4 applications) at 8-10 days interval. The crop debris should be ploughed down. Also, the resistant cultivars should be grown.

ii. Maydis leaf blight (MLB) MLB also occurs in wide range of maize growing states like Jammu & Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Sikkim, Meghalaya, Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka & Tamil Nadu. It shows the symptoms as lesions on the leaves elongated between the veins, tan, 2-6 x 3-22 mm with limited margins with buff to brown borders. For effective control of this disease, spray of Dithane Z-75 or Zineb @ 2.4 – 4.0 g/liter of water (2-4 applications) at 8-10 days interval after first appearance of symptoms of disease. In addition, the crop debris should be ploughed down. Also, the resistant cultivars should be grown. iii. Polysora Rust This disease appears mainly in peninsular India i.e Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. The main symptoms of the disease shows appearance of circular to elongate light cinnamon brown, circular to oval 0.2-2.0 mm long densely scattered legions on the upper leaf. The uredospores are yellowish to golden in colour. For effective control of polysora rust, three sprays of Dithane M-45 @ 2-2.5 gm/liter beginning from first appearance of symptoms at 15 days interval are required. It is always advisable to use resistant varieties.

iv. Banded leaf and sheath blight (BLSB) This disease mainly occurs in Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Sikkim, Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Delhi, Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. At appearance of the disease, white lesions develops on leaves and sheath. Purplish or brown horizontal bands present on white lesions characterize the disease. Seed treatment with peat based formulation (Pseudomonas fluorescence) @ 16 g/kg of seed or as soil application @ 7g/liter of water (soil drenching) or foliar spray of Sheethmar (Validamycin) @ 2.7 ml /liter water provides effective control of the disease. Stripping of 2 lower leaves along with leaf sheath also gives effective control of the disease. v. Post Flowering Stalk Rot of Maize (PFSR) The PFSR occurs mainly in Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Andhra Pradesh. Disease appears when the crop enters in senescence phase. The pathogen commonly affects the roots crown regions and lower internodes. When split open, the stalk shows pink-purple dis- colouration. For effective control of the disease, water stress at flowering should be avoided. Use balance dose of nutrients wherein potassium application helps in minimizing the disease. Use of bio-control agents (Trichoderma formulation) in furrows mixed with FYM @ 10g/kg at 10 days prior to its use in the field. It always advisable to practice crop rotation to minimize the disease incidence.

vi. Downy mildews (DM) Himachal Pradesh, Sikkim, West Bengal, Meghalaya, Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat are prone to downy mildews. The main symptoms of downy mildew are legends developing on lower leaves as narrow chlorosis strips. Strips extend in parallel fashion, well defined margined delimited by veins. Downy whitish to creamy growth usually on the ventral surface of the infected leaves appears corresponding to stripes. For control of downy mildew, the infected plants should be rogue out and destroyed. The planting of crop before onset of rains minimizes the incidence of mildew. Seed treatment with fungicides like Apron 35 WS @ 2.5 g/kg seed. Also the resistant varieties should be used. 11. Maize based cropping systems in India As maize has wide adaptability and compatibility under diverse soil and climatic conditions and hence it is cultivated in sequence with different crops under various agro-ecologies of the country. Hence, it is considered as one of the potential driver of crop diversification under different situation. Among different maize based cropping systems, maize-wheat ranks 1st having 1.8 m ha area mainly concentrated in rainfed ecologies. Maize-wheat is the 3rd most important cropping systems after rice-wheat and rice-rice that contributes about 3 % in the national food basket. The other major maize systems in India are maize-mustard, maize-chickpea, maize- maize, cotton-maize etc. Recently, due to changing scenario of natural resource base, rice-maize has emerged a potential maize based cropping system in peninsular and eastern India. In peri-

urban interface, maize based high value intercropping systems are also gaining importance due to market driven farming. Further, maize have compatibility with several crops of different growth habit that led to development of various intercropping systems. Studies carried out under various soil and climatic conditions under All India Coordinated Research Project on Cropping Systems revealed that compared to existing cropping systems like rice-wheat and rice-rice, maize based cropping systems are better user of available resources and the water use efficiency of maize based cropping systems was about 100 to 200 % higher at different locations. Maize and climate change Under the changing climate scenario the limitations of rising temperature during grain filling of wheat particularly in eastern India, and declining yield of boro rice in West Bengal and Orissa, water scarcity areas in peninsular India (AP and Tamil Nadu) affecting yield of Rabi rice, maize being a photo-insensitive crop has better options for adaptation and mitigation of these climatic changes. Peninsular India is considered to be a neutral environment for maize wherein maize can be cultivated in either of the seasons. Hence, maize has emerged as a potential as well as profitable crop in these areas. The rabi rice in Peninsular India and upland rice in Odisha and NEH region has low productivity. Therefore maize is only suitable alternative crop and more area is likely to shift towards maize cultivation in near future in these non- traditional areas. The various specialty corn types are quality protein maize (QPM), baby corn, sweet corn, pop corn, waxy corn, high oil corn etc. In India, QPM, baby corn and sweet corn are being popularized and cultivated by the large number of farmers. QPM which is nutritionally superior over the normal maize is the new dynamics to signify its importance not only for food and nutritional security but also for quality feed for poultry, piggery and animal sectors as well. Quality Protein Maize has specific features of having balanced amount of amino acids with high content of lysine and tryptophan and low content of leucine & isoleucine. Baby corn Baby corn is a young finger like unfertilized cobs with one to three centimeter emerged silk preferably harvested within 1-3 days of silk emergence depending upon the growing season. It can be eaten raw as salad and in preparation of different recipes such as chutney, pakora, mix vegetables, pickles, candy, murabba, kheer, halwa, raita, Chinese preparations, etc. The desirable size of baby corn is 6 to 11 cm length and 1.0 to 1.5 cm diameter with regular row/ ovule arrangement. The most preferred colour by the consumers / exporters is generally creamish to very light yellow. Baby corn is nutritive and its nutritional quality is at par or even superior to some of the seasonal vegetables. Besides proteins, vitamins and iron, it is one of the richest sources of phosphorus. It is a good source of fibrous protein and easy to digest. It is

almost free from residual effects of pesticides. It can be cultivated round the year therefore, three to four crops of baby corn can be taken in a year. Cost of cultivation of baby corn in India is lowest in the world therefore; India can become one of the major baby corn producing country. It has great potential both for internal consumption and export. In general, the cultivation practices of baby corn are similar to grain crop except (i) higher plant population (ii) higher dose of nitrogen application because of higher plant population (iii) preference for early maturing single cross hybrid and (iv)harvesting within 1-3 days of silk emergence. iii. It is becoming very popular in urban areas of country therefore, its cultivation is remunerative for peri-urban farmers. Besides green cobs the green fodder is also available to the farmers for their cattle. Generally sweet corn is early in maturity. It is harvested in 70-75 days during kharif season. Color: Sweet corn is generally dull yellow and white but dull yellow color is preferred. Precaution: Its picking should be done in the morning or evening time. Pop Corn Popcorn is one of the common snack items in many parts of the world, particularly in cities and is liked because of its light, porous and crunchy texture. The popcorn flour can also be used for preparing many traditional dishes. It is consumed fresh, as it has to be protected against moisture absorption from the air. It is hard endosperm flint maize. Kernels of pop corn are very small and oval/round in shape. When heated at about 1700C, the grains swell and burst, turning inside out. Quality of pop corn depends on popping volume and minimum number of non pop corn.

v. Waxy corn It is originated in China but largely used in USA. Grain gives wax-like appearance and having 100 % amylopectin starch. While in normal maize, the starch is nearly 30 percent amylose and the remaining 70 % is amylopectin. Waxy corn is mainly used for food and industrial purposes. vi. High oil corn Most of the normal maize lines have 3- 4 % oil content. In general, lines with more than 6 % oil are considered high oil lines. 95 % of the total oil is in the germ. When the oil percent increases the starch decreases. The wet milling industries are still in advantage with high oil content corn. In USA the high oil corn is cultivated on contractual basis and remunerative price is paid to the farmers. In India its cultivation is not economical because it is not sold on premium basis. Generally in normal maize crop, 15-20 % population of high oil hybrids is used as pollen parent and there is detasseling of the normal corn plant. Due to xenia effect there is an increase of oil in normal maize and its cultivation is done in isolation. The corn oil has low content of saturated fatty acid and is considered to be one of the best quality cooking oil. In India more than 60000 tonnes of corn oil is made available for various uses. vii. Isolation Distance Seed production should be taken in fertile well drained, weed and disease free soil and preferably the fields where preceding crop was not maize to minimize rouging and maintain the genetic purity. At least 400-500 metre distance is required to avoid any contamination.

ii. Male: female ratio The male: female ratio depends on (a) pollen shedding potential and duration of male parent; (b) male: female synchrony : for better seed setting flowering of female should be earlier than male or male pollen dehiscence should coincide with female silking and (c) season. In general the male: female ratio should be 1:2 or 1:3 or 1:4. iii. Time of Sowing To avoid flowering from heavy rains during kharif and low/high temperature during winter season the optimum time of sowing is first week of July during kharif and first week of November during winter. iv. Method of sowing and layout It is desirable to plant the crop on ridges. Depending upon the plant type the row and plant spacing should be kept at 60-75 cm and 20 cm, respectively. Identification labels/ tags should be put on the male and female lines to distinguish between them. v. Seed Rate The seed rate depends on size of seed/ test weight, plant type and male: female ratio. 15 kg ha-1 for female and 10 kg ha-1 for male is recommended. vi. Removal of off-type plants and thinning i) After 12-15 days of sowing: off-type and excess plants should be removed. Proper plant to plant distance should be maintained ii) At knee high stage all the dissimilar plants should be removed. iii) At flowering remove dissimilar tassel bearing plant before anthesis from the male. vii. Detasseling Detasseling in female should be done before anthesis. It should be practiced row-wise.

ii) At knee high stage all the dissimilar plants should be removed. iii) At flowering remove dissimilar tassel bearing plant before anthesis from the male. vii. Detasseling Detasseling in female should be done before anthesis. It should be practiced row-wise. One person should follow to monitor the each row to check that no part of the tassel is left inside. The process of detasseling should continue for 8-10 days. While detasseling, leaf should not be removed which will reduce the yield. It has been observed that the removal of 1 to 3 leaves along with tassel reduces 5-15 % yield. The removed tassel should not be thrown in the field but fed to the cattle as it is nutritive fodder. viii. Harvesting If possible male parent should be harvested after pollination. Optimum moisture content in grain at harvesting should be around 20 %. The harvested cobs should spread evenly instead of making heap. ix. Stages of crop inspection At the time of sowing: to monitor the land, isolation distance, planting ratio of male: female, proper sowing time, seed treatment During pre-flowering/vegetative stage: to verify the rouging and removal of off type plants During flowering stage: to check disease and pest infestation During post-flowering and pre-harvest stage: to remove the late and diseased plants Differential type of tassel/silk plants Harvesting time: to see the proper time of harvesting

x. Drying and sorting of seed parent cobs The drying of the cobs should not be done either on the kuccha or pucca flour, rather it should be dried on tarpoline sheets to avoid seed injury and during night the cobs should be kept covered. To maintain the purity, dissimilar, diseased and pest infested cobs should be removed before shelling. The female cobs should be dried up to 13-14 % moisture content before shelling. xi. Shelling Shelling of female parent should be done earlier than male to avoid mechanical mixture. Shelling can be done manually or by power operated maize Sheller. xii. Seed processing: All under size, broken, damaged etc seeds should be removed for maintaining the quality of seed. xiii. Storage and marketing Seed drying should be done till the moisture content of the seed is reduced to 8 % and it should be kept in aerated jute bags. Seed should be stored at cool and dry place preferably in cold storage. Poor storage conditions will lead to loss of vigour and poor germination. Marketing should be done with specifications and standards. 15. Data revealed that grain yield, yield attributes and physiological parameters remarkably varied with waterlogging stress among different maturity groups. The tolerance against waterlogging stress of EM and LM groups for plant stand resulted in higher average grain yield over other maturity groups. The mean grain yield of hybrids of different maturity groups differed significantly under normal and waterlogged conditions. Late maturity hybrid PMH-3 was to be the most tolerant against excess soil moisture stress (31.8 and 34.9% yield reduction) and medium maturity HM-9 was highly susceptible (55.2 and 64.6% yield reduction) during both years. Under temporary waterlogging condition, leaf diffusive resistance (LDR) and photosynthetic active radiation (PAR) showed positive correlation with grain yield while transpiration rate (TR) had negative correlation. SUMMARY Targeted scientific interventions for “Improvement of the livelihood and nutritional security of the tribal farmers through adoption of improved technology of maize production” were carried out by the team across different locations of North East states (Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim and Tripura) under TSP/NEH plan of ICAR- IIMR under two structured projects, viz., in collaboration with ICAR NEH Region under “Promoting improved technology of maize production in NEH Region” during 2015-21 and in collaboration with ICAR-NRCs on Pig, Yak and Mithun during 2018-19 and 2021-22 on “Maize production in NEH region for sustainable livestock production”. More than 20 improved technologies on participatory maize seed production, high yielding maize cultivars, liming, quality protein maize (QPM), baby corn and sweet corn, maize based integrated farming system, line sowing, optimum planting density, new intercropping systems (oilseed and pulses + maize), diversification of rice with maize for Jhum improvement, Jalkund integration with maize for double cropping, and zero tillage mustard were demonstrated. The entrepreneurship development opportunity through food processing and value addition in maize, maize silage baling, low cost hydroponics based maize fodder production, integrated pest management in maize etc. were introduced and successfully disseminated among the farmers, women SHGs, farmers club, NGOs and entrepreneurs. The integrated interventions changed the mindset of the people of 266 villages of 29 districts with direct benefit to 6919 tribal farmers in the NEH region covering 2711 hectare land. In addition to this, 109 trainings/workshop benefitted 9095 farmers/officials on improved maize

interventions changed the mindset of the people of 266 villages of 29 districts with direct benefit to 6919 tribal farmers in the NEH region covering 2711 hectare land. In addition to this, 109 trainings/workshop benefitted 9095 farmers/officials on improved maize farming system. With interventions of improved maize system, the cropping intensity increased from <100% to >185% with additional income ranging between Rs. 21,000 to 65,000 per ha. The maize based integrated farming system generated employment of 250 to 565 man-days per year per ha as compared to less than 100 days in rice based mono cropping system. Before intervention, 71.4 to 84.8% farmers were able to earn net returns <Rs. 60000/ha/year only. After technological intervention the net returns of the targeted farmers increased by 31.0-71.4% and net earnings enhanced up to Rs. 3 lakhs/ha/year. As 30-40% of the production was consumed at home, introduction and popularization of QPM, pulses and oilseed intercropping with maize increased the nutritional security and profitability among the tribal population. Similarly, the pulse availability/household varied from 0.7 to 1.1 t/annum. The farmer participatory maize seed production showed 60% production enhancement in NEH. The use of the QPM significantly improved the nutritional security and has further possibility of enhance pig, poultry and livestock 0

production with lesser maize requirement. The sweet corn and baby corn cultivation demonstrated to increase the livestock production without any extra requirement of land for fodder production. Among the various technologies participatory seed production, improved crop varieties, sweet corn and baby corn cultivation, quality protein maize, liming, Jalkund based maize integrated farming system and silage baling were adopted to the tune of 71.5-85% at fastest pace; followed by crop diversification in Jhum with maize+pulses, mustard under zero tillage after maize, maize for Jhum improvement with 63-68%. Meticulously trainings towards capacity building (23 training/workshop to 1897 officers/progressive farmers) against fall armyworm management in NEH region lead to successful control of this monster pest in NEH. The project made strengthening of seed system and cultivars development and SVRC released two cultivars (MZM-11, white maize and MZM-17, reddish pop corn) in Mizoram. Additionally, two cultivars identified for release by VIC (RCM 1-76 and RCM-1-61) in NEH region included in the demonstrations. A significant jump in the profitability (up to Rs 3 lakhs), cropping intensity (up to 300%) and employment generation (up to 500 man-days/annum) recorded with different technological intervention made by the team. The works accomplished has succeeded in showing the path to over 15000 resource poor tribal farming community for breaking the vicious cycle of low productivity-profitability-sustainability of hill farming system as well as food- nutritional-livelihood insecurity of the of NEH region. The team documented 19 scalable success

showing the path to over 15000 resource poor tribal farming community for breaking the vicious cycle of low productivity-profitability-sustainability of hill farming system as well as food- nutritional-livelihood insecurity of the of NEH region. The team documented 19 scalable success stories on maize in different cropping and farming systems in Manipur, Mizoram and Tripura. As an impact, the maize area in NEH increased by 6.59% which is higher than national level enhancement (2.12%) and the production also increased by 6.29% during the project period. We are thankful to all the project team members and directors from ICAR Research Complex for NEH region, NRCs on Yak, Pig and Mithun for their active participation and collaboration towards achieving desired outcome of the project. The last mile delivery help rendered by the KVKs of NEH region is also acknowledged. We hope the intervention made under this project will be helpful to replicate in NEH region for desired outcome towards improvement in livelihood security and resource sustainability. Authors 1

Conceptualization of the maize based intervention in NEH region The North Eastern Hilly (NEH) Region of India also known as the Eastern Himalayan region (EHR) extending from 21.5° to 29.5° North Latitude and 85.5° to 97.5° East Longitude between the foot hills of the Eastern Himalayas and the Patkai and Naga Hill Ranges and the altitude varies from almost sea-level to over 7,000 metres (23,000 ft) above MSL. Each state in northeast India touches an international boundary like Sikkim with China, Nepal, and Bhutan; Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh with China and Myanmar; Nagaland and Manipur with Myanmar; Meghalaya and Tripura with Bangladesh; and Assam with Bhutan. There are 145 tribal communities in NEH of which 78 are large each with >5000 population. They constitute around 12% of the total tribal population of India. In North East, main tribal groups includes Garos and Khasis of Meghalaya; Kukis and Nagas (Angami, Ao and Phom) of Manipur; Lushais of Tripura; Angami, Ao and Phom of Nagaland; and Lepchas of Sikkim. Northeast India is the homeland of a large number of tribes. The agriculture in the state is characterized by rugged terrain, wide variations in slopes and altitude, community land systems and traditional cultivation practices. Himalayan states of Sikkim and Arunachal have a cold climate while the rest on the gentle Purvachal ranges have hot humid summers, severe monsoons and mild winters. The agricultural production system in the state is mostly rainfed, monocropped and at subsistence

states of Sikkim and Arunachal have a cold climate while the rest on the gentle Purvachal ranges have hot humid summers, severe monsoons and mild winters. The agricultural production system in the state is mostly rainfed, monocropped and at subsistence level and have 0.74 m ha shifting cultivation area (current and abundant). The state has diverse climatic conditions from tropical to sub-temperate due to varying altitude. The NEH region has 8.3% geographical area and 4.0% (45 million) populations of India. Even with this very low population density, the NEH region produces only 1.1% of country’s food grain production and thus has a gap of 3% with population share. Owing to this, region is continues to be a net importer of food grains due to low penetration of improved cultivars and best management practices. About 70% of the total population of North East is engaged in agriculture and allied activities and it plays an important role in the social and economic life of people in North East, and will continue to do so in the near future. Majority of the population, predominantly tribal, is dependent on agriculture and land-based activities. The agricultural production system in the region is predominantly rainfed, mono- cropped at subsistence level. Slash and burn agriculture are still practiced in almost all the states except Sikkim on steep slopes with reduced cycle of 2-3 years as against 10-15 years in the past. Jat, Coordinator of Maize Project, ICAR-IIMR, Ludhiana; Dr. Meraj Alam Ansari, PI of Maize Project, ICAR Research Complex for NEH Region, Manipur Centre, Imphal; Dr. N. Prakash former Director of ICAR NEH and Dr. Sujay Rakshit were acted as Nodal Officer of the project. A multidisciplinary team of scientists of ICAR Research Complex for NEH Region (Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim and Tripura) and ICAR-IIMR, Punjab was constituted for implementing different activities under the said leadership. KVKs, Line Departments (Agriculture, Horticulture, Veterinary and Fishery), NGOs, SHGs and village institutions were involved in implementing the field activities. The entire programme was implemented based on following 10 points approaches: 1) Selection of villages, beneficiaries and prioritizing activities for each village cluster: During the period, several visits were made to different villages and interaction programmes were organized with village authority, district administration, KVKs and state government officials as well as local NGOs for analyzing the socio-economic profile of the farmers, prioritizing the activities in each and individual location and approaches for implementing the programme etc. Participatory Rural Appraisal (PRA) was organized on cluster basis where we personally touched a significant number of farmers to generate the first-hand information about local agro-ecosystem, livestock status, natural resources availability, farming practices, social structure and to identify the existing problems of farming community (Fig. 8). Similarly, we have standardized and popularized maize-pea, maize-mustard, maize-lentil cropping system under conservation agriculture and maize based IFS. Conservation agriculture for sustainable intensification: In another conservation agriculture experiment, it was observed that the maximum system productivity in terms of maize equivalent yield (MEY) under Conventional Tillage (CT) for vegetable cowpea followed by conventional tillage for maize + ricebean intercropping system (CT-CT) with their residues retention gave highest yield (7.3 t/ha) followed by CT-zero tillage (ZT) with their residue retention (6.04 Mg/ha). Zero tillage (CT-ZT) with residues retention penalize by 4.6 and 8.8% yield reduction, respectively as compared to CT-CT. Among land management practices, residue retention with CT-CT and ZT-ZT fetched the higher net returns as compared to residue removal in CT-CT. Zero tillage with residues retention reduce the energy use pattern (especially Direct nonrenewable energy) and decrease the carbon footprints, energy consumption, gas emission and maintain the soil health. Six varieties of maize namely African Tall, QPM (HQPM 1 & Shaktiman 5), sweet corn, babycorn, and Dirang local were cultivated in two different altitude, viz., in Dirang (5500 ft above msl) and Nyukmadung (9000 ft above msl) with or without using mulch and found out-standing growth of the African Tall variety at mid altitude (Dirang) than that of high altitude (Nyukmadung). It was recorded total production of 25,000- 30,000 kg/ha green fodder per cut @ 2.66 kg per m2. Amongst the grain verities, Dirang local variety shows the best results in Dirang campus in comparisons to both the varieties of QPM (Shaktiman 5 & HQPM 1) both in farm and field levels. Moreover, the productivity in other varieties like sweet corn and baby corn also shows satisfactory results. It was also observed all the varieties perform very poor in higher altitude i.e. Nyukmadung situated at 9000 ft above msl, but use of plastic mulch was found to be effective for improvement of maize productivity at high altitudes. Moreover, all these varieties were also tried in farmer‟s field and found satisfactory results. The maize green fodder cultivated during this period was utilized for feeding farm yaks. Besides, the surplus green maize fodder (almost 12-15 tons) were conserved through ensiling with or without mixing with other forages using concrete silo and polybags and evaluated their nutritive values in both lactating and growing yaks (IIMR Annual Report, 2020). Promotion of rain water harvesting for promoting rabi crops under maize based cropping system In the absence of major and medium irrigation potential/facilities, the alternative available method is to explore minor irrigation potential through effective water conservation measures. Due to lack of appropriate water management strategies, the irrigation potential of the state remains largely untapped and about 80% of the cultivated area is still rainfed. Therefore, to efficiently manage and harvest the rainwater for ensuring water availability during lean periods, concerted efforts have been made to popularize low cost rain water harvesting structure 'Jalkund' so that farmers can grow a second crop during the rabi season. Thus, 65 Jalkund established under earlier project (NICRA and TSP) in farmer‟s field by team member of ICAR Manipur centre with the objective to harvest the rain water in hilly terrains through a

a second crop during the rabi season. Thus, 65 Jalkund established under earlier project (NICRA and TSP) in farmer‟s field by team member of ICAR Manipur centre with the objective to harvest the rain water in hilly terrains through a small rain water harvesting structure Jalkund for increasing productivity, profitability and livelihood security (Fig. 36). The capacity of a Jalkunds for rain water harvest was varied from 45,000 (6  5  1.5 m) to 120000 (15  4  2 m) liters with establishment charges Rs. 6055-15000. On an average, the cost of per liter harvested water was computed at Rs. 0.067 per liter considering 3 years life span of lining material. Hence, the total water harvested from 2014-15 to 2017-18 through participatory Jalkund established by ICAR Complex Manipur Centre is almost 13.25 million liters (13250 M3) which otherwise goes as runoff and might create flood problems in the downstream areas. 36

The selected areas comprise hilly slopes, narrow valleys and terraced land containing a wide range of microclimate (tropical to sub-temperate). All the locations suffer from acute water scarcity during winter months. The majority of the farmers relied on rainfed crop production and they have not yet been exposed to improved varieties, scientific production technology, natural resource management and post harvest technology. Capacity building and skill enhancement of the farmers was emphasized throughout the implementation process. Community mobilization and integrated approach was the crux of this program. Integrated pest and disease management with special reference to management of Fall Armyworm in North East India Pest and diseases come in any cropping system. Best way to manage is to create awareness and initiation of control measures in a sustainable manner. In all training programmes lectures on diseases and pests of maize and their management were delivered. Literatures were distributed among the participants and extension agencies. Since beginning of 2019, incidence of a new invasive pest, fall armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda) (FAW) reported from various northeast states. Extensive awareness campaign was initiated involving farmers, extension agencies and other stakeholders. Since March 2019, a total 23 47

training/workshop/campaigns were organized benefitting 1897 officials/farmers. Prepared seven extension bulletins detailing identification, scouting and control measures of FAW were generated in English, Hindi and local languages. The concerted efforts lead by ICAR-IIMR in association with ICAR RC for NEH, ICAR-NBAIR and other agencies could contain the damage caused by FAW and its further spread due to established network of our project in the NEH. A few plants showing FAW damage need not warrant pesticide application; it would not be economical and environmental friendly. Thus, choice of pesticide used or not is given to be based on nature of damage, which depends upon size of larvae. Impact of crop diversification with inclusion of maize-pulses intercrop for Jhum improvement: The shifting cultivation is an indigenous land use system widely distributed and practiced in Manipur, where most of the farmers growing rice mixed farming, which is not productive, economical and sustainable. Impact on Improving productivity, profitability, employment, nutritional security and sustainability through maize integrated farming system: Integrated farming system has emerged as one of the important approaches of climate smart agriculture. To overcome the problems of resource poor farmers, a holistic, resource based, client oriented and interacting approach popularly known as integrated farming system (IFS) models were developed through participatory mode under different agro- 57

ecosystems (Fig. 55). Under the programme, four IFS were developed in Chandel (2), Churachandpur (1) and Thoubal (1). The models were developed following two approaches, first by utilizing the existing water body available with the farmers and second, by constructing water harvesting structure. The agriculture lands located at the periphery were used for crops and other components. The integrated farming systems model developed at farmers‟ field with the maize integration technology. The performance of each models consisting of agri (maize, pulses), horticulture, livestock, fisheries and secondary horticulture was evaluated for four consecutive years. The cropping intensity increased up to 180 to 300% compared to 120% in traditional farming system. The farming intensity has also been increased 300 to 500%, as compared to 150-200% in traditional farming system. On an average, 409 to 570 days employment was generated as compared to 110 days in traditional farming system. The average net return of various farming systems was increased to the tune of Rs. 1.76 to 5.03 lakh per annum over the traditional farming system. Fig. 55. Socio-economic Relevance: Targeting poverty: Poverty criteria were given priority at all stages of the implementation. Choice of area and target groups using PRA, baseline survey, selection of technologies and approaches were all influenced by poverty alleviation agenda which was critical to project success and development of pro- poor technology. This approach helped to sensitize all participants to poverty reduction issues and build a strong poverty orientation in their work. Critical mass: For farmers to play a larger role in participatory research and outreach, at every site a high number of farmers were engaged in the research process helping achieve a „critical‟ mass. Farmers were trained in data collection, systematic documentation, organizing fairs and focus group discussions. Food sovereignty: Farming communities of the region are known for their unusual adherence to specific taste. They grow large number traditional varieties to meet their taste requirement. In the present project, participatory crop and variety selection was given high priority from the beginning which helped in satisfying this need. Creating demand and supply: The programme helped to create both demand and supply for validated technologies. Capacity development programme organized To reach the needy, downtrodden tribal farmers in the remote villages of north east states several capacity building programs like training of farmers in small groups, mass campaign at village level, interface meet, field day, seed day, front line demonstrations etc. were conducted either at the village level or at the institute premises. Before undertaking any demonstration and on-farm participatory research activities, emphasis was given on upgradation of skill and knowledge of the beneficiaries. State level trainings in NEH region: We have organized 86 trainings in collaboration with respective line department officials and ICAR KVKs for the tribal maize growers in north east India (Table 15). The theme of the training programmes were concentrated on the scientific maize cultivation technologies for increasing profitability and resource use efficiency, integrated nutrient and water management, Liming for amelioration of soil acidity, adaptation of high yielding varieties (including sweet corn and baby corn cultivation), pest management techniques and post-harvest management under upland condition. Fodder maize cultivation potential was one of the prime aspects for improving livestock production for improving livelihood and nutrition security of marginal and small farmers in north east India (Fig. 61 to 65). Innovations Introduced The programme was conceptualized with an innovative idea to cover critical aspects of hill farming system in a holistic manner concentrating maize based farming. The important innovations introduced during implementation of the programmes are -  Introduction and popularization of high yielding varieties of maize (HQPM, Hybrids, high yielding composites). Altogether, 21 promising varieties of maize were identified and introduced in across the North east.  Revitalizing the varietal development, testing and release programme for maize in NEH region.  Introduction of baby corn and sweet corn for enhancing income and livestock productivity in NEH region.  Successful demonstration of participatory seed production programme through seed village concept in cross pollinated crop like maize. Maize (Zea mays) Varieties: Note: a) Seed from hybrid maize should not be kept as the crop deteriorates due to segregation. The seeds from composite can be used for three to four years without much deterioration in yield. b) All the above varieties are drought tolerant and resistant to most of the diseases to a fair degree. c) Excepting Diara, all other varieties/hybrids are suitable for all the zones except Barak Valley Zone. Selection of Site and Land Preparation: Any well drained soil is suitable for maize. Sandy and sandy loam fertile soils are preferable. It requires a deep fine and firm tilth. Manures and Fertilizers: A combination of organic and inorganic fertilizer gives better results than inorganic fertilizer alone. Compost or FYM @ 5 t/ha should be applied For Hills Zone, a dose of 90 : 40 : 40 kg/NPK per hectare is recommended under rainfed condition. 33

Method of Fertilizer Application: FYM or compost should be applied during land preparation. The entire quantity of SSP and MOP and half of the total urea is to be applied in furrows (8-10 cm deep) and covered with 4-5cm of soil. Sowing of seed should be done atleast 2 days after fertilizer application. There remaining half of urea should be top dressed in two equal doses followed by earthing up; in each case. The first ¼ at 35 days after germination or when the plants are at knee high stage and the second ¼ at the tasselinitiationst age of the crop i.e. 45- 60 days after germination or at the time of elongation of the flag leaf which ever is earlier. The fertilizer should be applied on both sides of row and weeds should also be removed from the field during this operation. However, before application of the fertilizer a light hoeing is to be given between the lines 2-3days ahead. Seed Rate: Depending upon the seed size about 18-22.5 kg of seeds/ha (2.5-3 kg/ bigha) are required. Seed Treatment: Seeds should be dressed with Carboxin @ 2 g/kg of seed Sowing Time: * Refer to page iii for full forms of agro-climatic zones **July and August for late planting in hills. Method of Sowing: Seeds should be dibbled at a depth of 3-4 cm in rows 65-75 cm apart and at a distance

Refer to page iii for full forms of agro-climatic zones **July and August for late planting in hills. Method of Sowing: Seeds should be dibbled at a depth of 3-4 cm in rows 65-75 cm apart and at a distance of 20-25 cm from seed to seed within the rows. Two seeds per hill are to be sown followed by thinning10 days after germination retaining one seedling/ hill. Depending upon the fertility status of the soil, a wider spacing can be used. Varieties like Diara can be sown at closer spacing because of their short stature and shorter duration. Weeding and Inter-culture: Light hoeing and earthing up should be done as and when necessary. For further and adequate control of weed, simazine should be applied @ 0.5 – 1.0 kg a.i/ha in 1000 lit of water a pre-emergence spray. Irrigation and Drainage: Maize is primarily grown as rainfed crop; but application of irrigation at the time of soil moisture deficit ensures optimum yield. Silking stages and grain filling period are the 34

two critical stage of the maize crop. Excess rain water can be drained out through surface drainage channel of 25 cm width, 15 cm deep spaced at 6 m distance. Water Management Maize should be sown in paired rows of 50 cm between pair and 70 cm gap is to be given between two pairs. Two rows of black gram should be sown in between two pairs of maize Plant Protection: When infestation of stem borer is noticed, fipronil 5 SC @ 1.0 kg/ha in 200-250 lit of water should be sprayed with power sprayer or in 700-800 lit of water with hand sprayer. In areas where banded sclerotial disease (Rhizoctonia solani) is noticed, the plants should be sprayed with hexaconazole 5EC @ 2ml/lit of water at an interval of 12-15 days. Matured cobs can be protected from bird damage by tying cobs with leaves of the same plant. Harvesting: Harvesting should be done as soon as the husk covers turn brown and the silks are completely dry. Harvesting immediately after a shower should be avoided. Ears (cobs) should be thoroughly dried in the sun before shelling or storing unshelled. 35

FOREWORD Maize is the largest produced cereal in the world with 1148 mt production with average productivity of 5.9 t/ha, which is the highest. The growth rate of maze is also one among the highest. The crop is spreading very fast to non-traditional areas like peninsular, central and eastern India. This is due to its increased market demand both by multifarious uses as food, feed, fodder and raw material for large number of industrial products besides use in bioethanol production, it is the best suited crop to double farmers' the rice-based cropping system. Convervation agriculture practices have been largely been very successful in maize-based cropping system, with higher system productivity and profitability. However, labour shortage and higher input prices are making agriculture less remunerative in present context in India. Thus, the use of machineries for crop cultivation is much needed for sustainable production specially the crop like maize that is fast spreading in India. Maize being widely spaced and dominated by single cross hybrids with uniform ear placement and maturity, it is suitable for mechanized cultivation. Maize cultivation is completely mechanized in the major producing countries like USA and China but unlike rice and whear in India, mechanization in maize cultivation is penetrating at slower pace. It is primarily due to less awareness about applicability of mechanization of maize cultivation an d availability of these machines at farmers' doorsteps. The use of machines for various cultivation practices will help in augmenting the profitability of maize cultivation, reduction of drudgery and improved health of farmers. The mechanization of maize cultivation will help in its faster adoption and enhanced production to meet the future requirement of maize in the country. PREFACE During the last few decades, the agriculture sector in India has witnessed a drop in the labor availability mainly due to increased job opportunities in service and manufacturing sectors. These declining trends of agricultural labor and raising wages calling for automatic or semi-automatic farm machineries to perform various crop productions tasks. In India, nearly 80 percent of maize is grown in rain fed region where all the agriculture operations are rain depended and need to be carried out in short time span. Intensive cropping systems particularly in irrigated regions require quick land preparation, seeding and harvesting to incorporate more number of crop in a year. Hence, mechanization is very much in demand in both rain fed and irrigated maize. But, the mechanized maize cultivation is not much popular due to lack of awareness about farm machineries. Hence, to spread awareness about mechanization, different farmers friendly machineries and supportive govt. schemes; a bulletin entitled with ''Mechanized maize production for enhanced productivity and profitability'' has been written. This bulletin broadly covered need of mechanization in Indian agriculture and particularly for maize crop; important tractor drawn machineries for land preparation, planting, weeding, fertilizer application, harvesting, and post-harvest operations. Animal drawn, manually or power operated machineries that suit the financial status of small and marginal farmers has also been described. It is hoped that this information will be pretty useful to all the maize growers in the country. March 2020 Authors Ludhiana

Introduction Agriculture is the third most important sector of Indian economy with 18 percent share in gross domestic product (GDP). Agriculture is the most important source of livelihood and support nearly 50 percent of Indian population. After the economic reforms of 1990s, spectacular changes were noticed in sector wise share in employment as a result in employment generation in the secondary and tertiary sectors. In 1991, agriculture alone was providing 63 percent employment which dropped to 59.9, 56.7, 53.3 and 48.8 percent in 1999-00, 2004-05, 2009-10 and 2011-12, respectively (Fig.1). The expansion of public works like Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Generation Act (MGNREGA) 2005 and migration of rural population to the cities and abroad in search of employment is other reason for labour shortage in agriculture. As a result share agricultural labour to the total labour force dropped to 43.2% in ten years from 2009 leading to crisis of shortage of labour in agricultural practices. With higher education more labour forces are moving to the industry and service sectors. Agriculture activities being more tiring with lesser social repute there is further possibility for decline in agriculture work force in coming years. Further, agricultural practices being seasonal in nature do not provide regular employment, and on the contrary has peak labour demand during sowing, weeding and harvesting. Mechanization is defined as application of machine power instead of draught animals or human labour to complete agricultural tasks. Mechanization increases the speed of agricultural practices and saves time and labour in farming operations. It lowers production cost and improves farm income. Mechanization of farm operations can shift agriculture from 'subsistence farming' to 'commercial agriculture'. Advantages of Mechanization Ø Timely and speedy farm operations Ø Crop intensification Ø Reduced labour drudgery Ø Reduced cost of cultivation Ø Increase per day and per manpower productivity Ø Quality produce Ø Improve living standard Ø Saving of fuel, labour, natural resources, eco-friendly Maize is a multifaceted crop grown in varied agro-climatic conditions for food, fodder, feed and industrial purpose globally. Worldwide, maize is cultivated in nearly 185 mha area along with a production of above 1070 mt and average productivity of 5.6 t/ha. In India, this coarse grain is currently being cultivated on 9.6 mha with 28.26 mt production. Among the cereals, maize is the most resource-use efficient and high yielding crop and is extensively used in livestock sector as feed (piggery, poultry, fishery etc.) and fodder. Among field crops maize can best integrated with livestock and poultry components ensuring an integrated farming system, (the core for doubling farmers income. Demand of this crop is rising every year and in future also its demand will be higher due to dietary shift towards non-vegetarian foods.

Why mechanization in maize? Maize crop suits to mechanization: Maize seeds being relatively bolder as compared to other crops and being wide spaced crop allows tractor to move in the field enabling tractor-based sowing to intercultural operations. Maize cobs are placed well above the ground is amenable to harvesting mechanically. Post-harvest operations like dehusking, shelling, drying etc. are quite labour intensive and amenable to mechanized interventions. Thus, seed to seed mechanization can be successful in maize and much progress in this regard has already been made. Availability of maize cultivars amenable to mechanization: Predominant cultivars in maize in India till mid 1990s were composites and synthetics. Such cultivars have non-synchronous maturity and uneven ear placement. Both these parameters are not suitable for mechanized operations. Double cross hybrids though higher in productivity than composites and synthetics, have the inherent limitations of uneven maturity and cob placement. On the other hand, single cross hybrids, which have made large scale inroads in the maize cultivation scenario since beginning of this millennium, are uniform in plant type, seed characters, maturity and ear placement. Thus, such cultivars suit best for mechanization from seed to seed. Maize as commercial crop: Traditionally maize in India used to be consumed as food crop. However, over time maize has become more an industrial crop rather food crop. This is because over 75 % of the maize produced in India is used for industrial purchases (Rakshit et al. 2017)

Maize utilization pattern in India

Non-traditional areas under maize cultivation: Maize in India was a kharif crop of north western India in the states of Punjab, Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh. Since mid 1980s there was a gradual shift in maize cultivation, when it made inroads more in peninsular India and losing its major footprint in northwestern India. Currently the peninsular India contributes to over 50 percent of maize production from around 40 percent national maize area. Further, with its continued demand, particularly in poultry and starch industry it is fast spreading to non-traditional areas like West Bengal, rice fallows and coastal belt having mechanized cultivation of other crops, viz., rice, wheat etc. To increase farm profitability in such situations mechanized cultivation is the need of the hour. Maize as rain-fed crop: Over 75 percent of maize in India is (grown as rain-fed crop where operations like sowing, weeding, earthing up etc. are often affected by the rainfall providing little window period to perform these operations. Mechanized cultivation enables conduct of these critical operations on time and reduces drudgery. Further, it enhances farm profitability of rain-fed maize production. Intensive cropping systems: With increasing demand from agriculture of more produce from less land, intensification of cropping system is the only alternative. Intensive cropping systems particularly in irrigated regions need quick harvesting for timely seeding of successive crop. Here mechanized harvesting as well as land preparation and sowing are very much in demand. Rain at harvesting: Rain/thunder storms at harvesting can destroy the whole season efforts of

irrigated regions need quick harvesting for timely seeding of successive crop. Here mechanized harvesting as well as land preparation and sowing are very much in demand. Rain at harvesting: Rain/thunder storms at harvesting can destroy the whole season efforts of farmers. Further, untimely rain during harvesting or while drying maize cobs/grains lead to higher grain moisture leading to risk of aflatoxin. Under this situation mechanized harvesting, dehusking, shelling and drying can very effectively address the issue of aflatoxin, ensuring higher selling price. Declining agricultural labour in traditional areas: It has already been highlighted previously that availability of agricultural labours is in decreasing trend, which hinders timely farm operations, and make the operations costly. The declining trend of labour in agriculture highlighted the need of farm mechanization in every crop including maize. Higher labour cost: Labour requirement in different maize growing states ranges between 431 to 753 man hour per ha, which contribute approximately 39-64 percent of total operational cost (Table 1). As large part of cost of cultivation is shared by labour only, hence adoption of mechanization can potentially reduce the requirement of labour and reduce the production cost.

Equipments for mechanization In order to make maize cultivation more economic mechanization from seed to seed is the best option. The level of mechanization varies from place to place, cropping system to system and size of farming. However, unlike rice and wheat mechanization in maize is less popular and less in practice. 1) Tillage and seedbed preparation Tillage is the mechanical opening of soil to prepare a seed bed for proper germination and good growth of plants. Tillage is power intensive operation mainly carried out by tractor or animal drawn plough, cultivator and harrows. Tillage implements are broadly classified as primary and secondary implements. Under primary tillage, cutting and turning of furrow slice is carried out to pulverize the soil. It also helps in burying weeds and weed seeds, and disease propagules in deeper layers. In secondary tillage, harrow/cultivator etc. is used to crush larger clods followed by smoothing/leveling of field. These operations help in good seed germination and uniform crop stand and maturity. Mould Board (MB) Plough: It is primary tillage equipment which turn the soil, cuts trashes and buries them inside the soil. It is also used for turning and mixing green manure crops/ compost/farmyard manure, lime and other soil amendments into the soil. These 4-5 runs of tractors and tractor attached heavy tools, press the soil particles affecting soil structure, and create compaction problem which hinder seedling emergence, root penetration, soil aeration and water movement. This technology is very common in the U.S.A, Canada, Argentina and Australia. In India zero till maize planting has been adopted in coastal Andhra Pradesh in rice-maize system. This technology saves diesel, tractor's working time and labor enabling timely sowing of crops. If zero planting is combined with residue mulching, it modifies hydro-thermal properties and protects the crop during adverse conditions. Rotary weeder 6) Irrigation Utilization of electricity/diesel operated water lifting pumps reduces labour and time required to lift water and cover bigger crop area. Although, maize in India is basically a rain-fed crop, in some ecologies, particularly during rabi season it is grown with irrigation. Flooding or furrow method is more common for maize cultivation. These surface methods of irrigation need precise land leveling and water-guidance channel for uniform water distribution. These conventional irrigation methods are labor-intensive especially for irrigation channel construction, maintenance and operation. Such systems are also less efficient in water economy. Drip irrigation does not need leveling, channel formation and channel maintenance. Farmers do not have to hire labour for irrigation as they can operate the drip irrigation system by push of a switch. Simultaneous application of water and other inputs like fertilizer, insecticide and herbicide through drip lines are also possible which save labour and cost of application of agri-inputs. Sprinkler irrigation is possible till 10-12 leaves stage of the crop. This also can save water but involves some amount of labour to fix and move pipes and sprinklers.

PREFACE Welcome to the technical bulletin titled "Specialty Maize Cultivation Practices for Livelihood Security". Maize (Zea mays L.) has long held a prominent position in global agriculture, contributing significantly to food security, economic stability, and various industrial applications. This versatile cereal crop, cultivated on approximately 197 million hectares worldwide, plays a pivotal role in sustaining the agricultural landscape. In India, maize ranks as the third most important crop, earning it the title of the 'Queen of cereals' due to its exceptional yield potential among cereals. Maize's adaptability to diverse climates, from tropical to temperate, combined with its C4 classification, has made it a resilient and consistent performer in Indian agriculture. In recent years, India has witnessed remarkable growth in maize production, achieving record-breaking numbers that underscore its importance. The cultivation of maize in India predominantly occurs during the kharif season, representing 78% of the total acreage. However, the rabi season, despite its smaller acreage share (22%), significantly contributes to overall production. This dynamic is driven by various factors, including demand from the feed, starch, processed food, silage, and ethanol industries, all of which rely heavily on maize. As maize production continues to rise, it becomes increasingly vital to optimize its cultivation practices, particularly during the kharif season, which accounts for the majority of acreage but lags behind in productivity compared to rabi maize. Addressing this productivity gap and achieving consistent and sustainable growth in maize production is imperative to meet the burgeoning demand.

It surpasses all other food crops in its ability to adapt to the diverse agro- ecological niches and being cultivated from 58° N to 55° S latitude. In India, it holds third rank among the cereals, after rice and wheat in terms of area and production. Traditionally, maize is grown as a kharif crop in India, but from 1970s its expansion started in rabi season and later on in the spring season too. Now, the crop is grown round the year and in all agro-ecologies throughout India. Traditionally maize in India used to be consumed as food crop. However, over time maize has become rather an industrial crop than food crop as over 75% of the maize produced in India is used for industrial purchases, mostly as feed and source of starches. Being industrial in nature maize can ensure higher remuneration. Other than grain, maize is also cultivated for various purposes like quality protein maize (QPM), and other special purposes known as 'Specialty Corn'. The various specialty corn types are QPM, baby corn, sweet corn, pop corn, waxy corn, high oil corn etc. In India, QPM, baby corn and sweet corn are being popularized and cultivated by the large number of farmers. It offers advantages such as substituting costly high-protein supplements like soybean or fish meal. Feeding trials revealed that rats fed on opaque-2 maize exhibited substantial weight gain and improved feed efficiency. In poultry, QPM, when supplemented with methionine, outperformed regular maize in terms of growth, weight gain, and feed conversion, highlighting its promise as a valuable poultry feed. QPM production technology The production technology of QPM is same as of normal grain maize except isolation. To maintain the purity of QPM, it should be grown in isolation with normal maize. Field preparation The QPM crop requires terrain that is adequately aerated, wet, and weed-free. Land preparation comprises one deep ploughing on light-textured soils immediately after the previous winter/summer crop to ensure the timely sowing of the crop. If the soil is heavy, 2-3 deep ploughings at a depth of 50-60cm may be required. Generally, the crop requires 2-4 harrowing followed by planking to make the field clod-free and the best- suited texture for the germination of the crop. During the kharif season, the crop needs to be protected against waterlogging, so shallow furrows should be installed after a specific distance and connected to the main drain. Specialty Maize Cultivation Practices for Livelihood Security  Sowing method and seed rate In kharif sown maize, raised bed planting is recommended to protect the crop from water logging. Southern side planting is advised on East-West oriented ridge. For proper germination and early vigor, seed should be sown at 3.5-5.0 cm depth. Optimum plant density (33,000/acre) should be maintained by growing the crop at 60 × 20 cm row × plant spacing. Eight kg seed of QPM is needed for planting in one acre area. Prior to sowing, seeds should be treated with fungicides and insecticides to protect the crop from most prevalent seed and soil borne diseases and insect-pests. Specialty Maize Cultivation Practices for Livelihood Security  Water management QPM crops require an optimal water supply ranging from 400 to 600 mm. High or low moisture contents can hinder crop development. Ensuring better crop performance primarily hinges on effective drainage to manage excess water and meeting the crop's requirements during critical growth stages. Adequate moisture at germination, pre- tasseling, silking and grain-filling stages should be ensured through irrigation. If available, the sprinkler irrigation up to knee length stage is very good for maize crop. In ridge-sown crop, irrigation should be given in furrow up to 2/3rd of height of the ridge. When there is little water available, irrigation can be done in alternate furrows without much of a negative impact on the crop output. Weed management Weed is one of the significant biotic elements that hinder achieving the productive capacity of maize crop. The percentage of yield losses, which ranges from 25-80%, is greatly influenced by the type of weeds present, the length of the crop-weed competition, and the density of weeds. To reduce the damaging impacts of weeds on agricultural plants, the integration of weed management approaches, combining cultural, mechanical, chemical, and biological techniques, is recommended. Cultural weed control: Cultural practices play an important role in weed management in maize crops. It comprises several approaches like the selection of a competitive crop variety having well-adaptability and better vigour with appropriate disease and pest resistance; modern tillage practices like zero tillage involving residue cover; appropriate

role in weed management in maize crops. It comprises several approaches like the selection of a competitive crop variety having well-adaptability and better vigour with appropriate disease and pest resistance; modern tillage practices like zero tillage involving residue cover; appropriate planting time and density; the placement of right amount of nutrient at proper growth stages; adoption of narrower row spacing than conventional system along with suitable crop rotation including cover crops. Mechanical weed control: After the crop has been sown, weeds are frequently removed with an inter-row cultivator or a rotary hoe during in-row cultivation. Mechanical weed control using tractor mounted implements can only be done during the early crop stages because limited tractor and cultivator ground clearance damage the crop foliage at later growth stages. Working depth of weeding implements should be shallow to prevent plant roots damage. In the western Himalayan region, ploughing in standing crops at 20–25 days of development is referred to as "haloding," which aids in weed uprooting and earthing-up of plants. Additionally, this aids in the creation of furrows, which hold onto precipitation and support the crop during dry spells. Chemical weed management: Using pesticides to manage weeds in corn is the most crucial step. Herbicides can be sprayed at various times, including before the crop is planted (pre-plant incorporation), after the crop is planted but before emergence (pre- emergence), and following crop emergence (postemergence). 6

Specialty Maize Cultivation Practices for Livelihood Security  Pest management Fall armyworm, maize stem borer, pink stem borer and shoot fly are the four most significant pests affecting QPM crop in India. Maize stem borer infests during the kharif season, pink stem borer in the rabi season, and shoot fly during the spring season. For effective management of stem borers in maize crops, it is advisable to apply Chlorantraniliprole 18.5% SC at a rate of 60 ml per acre between 15-18 days after sowing. Seed treatment with Imidacloprid 600 FS (Gaucho) @ 6 ml /kg or Thiamethoxam 30 FS @ 8ml/kg seed is recommended to control shoot fly. Whorl application of any one of the insecticides viz., Chlorantraniliprole 18.5% SC (80 ml/acre) @ 0.4 ml/L; Thiamethoxam 12.6 % + Lambda cyhalothrin 9.5% ZC (50 ml/acre) @ 0.25 ml/L; Spinetoram 11.7 % SC (100 ml/acre) @ 0.5 ml/L; Emamectin benzoate5% SG (80 g/acre) @ 0.4g/L is recommended for fall army worm management. Harvesting and yield The optimal time for QPM harvesting is when the kernels are fully mature and have reached the desired moisture content (20-30%) and cob husk has dried and turned brown. After harvesting, sun-dry the cobs before proceeding with the shelling process. Specialty Maize Cultivation Practices for Livelihood Security  Sowing time Baby corn can be cultivated throughout the year provided the temperature remains above 20-28°C. Under Northern Indian conditions, where winters are quite cold, it's recommended to raise baby corn nurseries inside polyhouses during January, with subsequent transplantation in early February. Crops sown between August to November tend to be more productive, yielding a greater number of harvests. Winter-sown crops fetches higher prices in the market due to reduced competition during this period. Staggered sowing of baby corn is advised to ensure a continuous and extended harvest of baby corn rather than having all the corn mature simultaneously. Sowing method and seed rate The crop is typically planted on southern side of ridges following row-to-row spacing of 60 cm and a plant-to-plant spacing of 15 cm. Raised bed planting of baby corn is also popular among the farmers, where they accommodate two rows of baby corn on a 90 cm wide bed. Approximately 9-10 kg of seed is needed for planting one acre of baby corn. Baby corn planted on raised bed 13

Specialty Maize Cultivation Practices for Livelihood Security  Intercropping In general, short duration varieties of intercrops to be preferred for intercropping with baby corn. In kharif season, cowpea for green pods and fodder purposes and coriander for green leaves can be intercropped with baby corn. During rabi season, baby corn can be intercropped with vegetable crops, viz., spinach, cabbage, cauliflower, coriander, fenugreek, sugar beet, potato, radish etc. Recommended dose of fertilizers of intercrops should be applied in addition to the recommended dose of fertilizers of baby corn. Fig. Baby corn based intercropping Isolation requirement Baby corn crop needs isolation of at least 400 m from normal maize as pollination deteriorates its quality. Nutrient management Apply appropriate fertilizers based on soil testing and the nutrient requirements of baby corn. Generally, 60-70: 25:25 kg/acre N:P:K should be applied. Specialty Maize Cultivation Practices for Livelihood Security  Irrigation management Irrigation is a critical aspect of baby corn cultivation as it directly influences crop growth, yield, and quality. Seedling stage, knee high stage, silking and picking are the most sensitive stages for water stress and irrigation should be ensured at these stages. Light and frequent irrigations are desirable for the crop. Detasseling & Harvesting Tasseling and fertilization diminish the quality of baby corn, and a yield penalty is incurred as a substantial portion of the plant's energy is redirected toward tassel development. Therefore, it is crucial to promptly remove these tassels as soon as they emerge from the flag leaf. De-tasseling should be practiced row-wise. During de- tasseling leaf should not be removed otherwise it hamper baby corn yield. The removed tassels should not be thrown in the field as they possess nutritional values thus must be fed to cattle. Detasseling is not required in male-sterile varieties like Shishu. Specialty Maize Cultivation Practices for Livelihood Security  Baby corn is typically harvested 1-3 days after the silk emerges, at a point when the silk measures approximately 1-2 cm in length. For optimal yield and quality, it is advisable to conduct pickings daily during kharif and on alternate day during rabi season. Baby corn picking should be done in morning or evening hours when temperature and moisture conditions are favorable. During the Kharif season, about 3-5 pickings, while in the rabi season, 6-7 pickings from a baby corn crop may be obtained. The cultivation of baby corn generates various by-products, including tassels, silk, husks, and green plant material after harvest. These by-products are rich in nutrients and can serve as excellent cattle feed, contributing to increased milk yield. Specialty Maize Cultivation Practices for Livelihood Security  Post-harvest management To fetch good market price, baby corn needs some post-harvest treatments like de- husking, de-silking, grading and packing. Peel the baby corn by removing its silk and husk. After peeling, baby corn of uniform size and colour should be separated for packing. The packing material should be new and clean and should avoid external damage to the produce. Poly bags, terra pack, tray pack etc. can be used for packing. De-husked baby corn can be stored for a period of 6-7 days under conditions of low temperature (around 5- 6 ?C) and high humidity (~90 % relative humidity). To extend the shelf life of the produce and facilitate long-term storage and transportation over long distances, processes such as canning, dehydration, and freezing can be done. Grading and packing of baby corn Processing Baby corn can be processed to improve its shelf life. Processing involves various methods and techniques that help preserve the quality and extend the storage life of baby corn. Some common methods of processing baby corn for improved shelf life include: Canning: Baby corn can be canned, which involves sealing it in airtight containers after blanching or cooking. This process helps to kill bacteria, yeast, and molds, thereby extending the shelf life of the baby corn for several months or even years. Canning is the most commonly used method for processing of baby corn. Freezing: Baby corn can also be frozen to preserve its freshness. Freezing prevents the

extending the shelf life of the baby corn for several months or even years. Canning is the most commonly used method for processing of baby corn. Freezing: Baby corn can also be frozen to preserve its freshness. Freezing prevents the growth of microorganisms and enzymatic reactions that can cause spoilage. It typically maintains the quality of the corn for a longer period compared to other methods. Pickling: Baby corn can be pickled in vinegar or brine solutions. Pickling helps to create an acidic environment that inhibits the growth of spoilage microorganisms and enhances the shelf life while adding flavor. Drying/Dehydration: Baby corn can be dried to reduce its moisture content, making it less susceptible to spoilage. Dried baby corn can be stored for an extended period and rehydrated before use. Blanching: Blanching involves briefly immersing baby corn in boiling water, which helps to inactivate enzymes that can cause deterioration. After blanching, the corn can be canned, frozen, or dried. 17

Specialty Maize Cultivation Practices for Livelihood Security  Preservatives: Food-grade preservatives, such as citric acid or ascorbic acid (vitamin C), can be added to baby corn products to inhibit microbial growth and oxidative reactions, extending their shelf life. Modified Atmosphere Packaging (MAP): In this method, the air inside the packaging is modified to reduce oxygen levels and increase carbon dioxide levels. This can slow down the deterioration of baby corn. Vacuum Packaging: Vacuum packaging removes air from the packaging, creating a low- oxygen environment that can help preserve the baby corn's quality and shelf life. The choice of processing method depends on factors such as the desired shelf life, intended use of the baby corn, and the resources available. Advantages of baby corn cultivation Employment generation: The process of baby corn harvesting is labour-intensive and relies on manual operations, providing employment opportunities for rural communities. Additionally, post-harvest tasks such as de-husking, desilking, grading, and packing create jobs for a significant number of individuals. Regular income: Year-round sales of baby corn, corn straw, inter-crops, and similar agricultural products can offer a consistent source of income to farmers. Higher profitability: A single baby corn crop can yield earnings of up to Rs. 22,500 per acre in a short span of 2-2.5 months, along with a substantial green fodder production of 150 q per acre. Fodder for livestock: By-products of baby corn like maize stalk, tassel, silk and husk can

up to Rs. 22,500 per acre in a short span of 2-2.5 months, along with a substantial green fodder production of 150 q per acre. Fodder for livestock: By-products of baby corn like maize stalk, tassel, silk and husk can be utilized as valuable green fodder. This ensures a year-round supply of green fodder for milch animals without incurring any additional costs. Sweet corn kernels are typically plump, tender, and juicy with sweet taste, attributed to its higher sugar content compared to field corn. They can vary in color, including yellow, white, and bi-color varieties. Sweet corn is a very delicious and rich source of energy, vitamin C and A. It is eaten as raw, boiled or steamed green cobs/ grain. It is also used in preparation of soup, salad and other recipes. It is becoming very popular in urban areas of country therefore; its cultivation is remunerative for peri- urban farmers. Besides green cobs, the green fodder is also available to the farmers for their 18

Sweet corn production technologies Site selection Sweet corn is well-suited for peri urban agriculture because it should be consumed soon after harvest. Areas chosen for sweet corn cultivation should have convenient access to irrigation facilities. Sweet corn crop needs isolation of at least 250 m from normal maize/popcorn as pollination deteriorates its quality. Sweet corn varieties: Zone-wise recently released sweet corn varieties are listed below: Sowing time The ideal planting time is June-July in kharif (rainy) and September-October in rabi (winter) season. An increase in temperature to over 35°C during tasseling can result in tassel blast and reduced grain setting. Moreover, at high temperature due to conversion of fructose into polysaccharides sweet corn losses flavour. Due to these reasons, sweet corn cultivation should be avoided during spring season. In Northern Indian conditions, sweet corn planting should be avoided between 15th November to 20th January, when temperature remains below 16°C. conditions, sweet corn planting should be avoided between 15th November to 20th January, when temperature remains below 16°C. Instead, its nursery can be prepared in tunnels using coco pit and subsequently transplanting can be done after 20th January when temperature goes above 10?C. Implementing staggered planting of sweet corn with intervals of 7-10 days ensure a continuous supply to the market and consequently higher returns. Sowing method and seed rate The crop is sown at 75 cm row-row spacing and 25-30 cm intra-row spacing. Approximately, 2.5-3 kg seed/acre is required to accommodate recommended plant population of 18,000 to 21,000 plants per acre.
